He was Professor of Politics and International Relations at the University of New South Wales from 1996 until retirement in 2012. He has a long-time interest in the philosophy of Ludwig Wittgenstein, its implications for the practice of social science, and its relationship Karl Marx’s philosophical ideas. ==Academic and fiction work== Early in his career Kitching worked in the inter-disciplinary field of Development Studies, wrote a best-selling introductory text, ''Development and Underdevelopment in Historical Perspective'' (1989). He specialised in the study of economic and political development in Africa. His Oxford D Phil thesis was a participant observation study of peasant agriculture in a northern Tanzanian village, and in 1981 he Herskovitz Award of the US African Studies Association for his book ''Class and Economic Change in Kenya''. This was a widely praised study of the commercialisation of peasant agriculture in Kenya and its effects on the country’s African population. In the late conducted field research in Russia the de-collectivisation of agriculture following the collapse of the USSR. Following his retirement from academic life Gavin has continued to write about the importance of Wittgenstein’s ideas for social scientists and researchers. He has written history of football (soccer) in the North-East of England, his region of birth. As well as his academic books and articles, Kitching has also written some fiction (both and plays) and these listed below. However, although he is proud of his academic publications, which are are widely recognised and appreciated, he would not make similar claims for his fiction. He played [[]first-class cricket]] [removed: er] [added: for [[Assam cricket team|Assam]]] and [removed: cricket coach. A left-arm [[orthodox spin]]ner and left-handed middle-order batsman, he played first-class cricket for] [[Delhi cricket team|Delhi]] [added: between 1986] and [removed: [[Assam cricket team|Assam]] across two decades, representing India at the Under-19 level and competing in all of India's premier domestic tournaments] [added: 2005]. [removed: He is also widely recognised for his decade-long career as an [[overseas professional]] cricketer in England and his subsequent career as a [[BCCI]]-certified coach and cricket administrator. ==Early life and education== Singh was born on 23 February 1967 in [[Jalandhar]], Punjab, India. He completed his secondary education at Sardar Patel Vidyalaya, New Delhi (CBSE, 1986), and later graduated from [[SGTB Khalsa College]], [[University of Delhi]]. ==Playing career== ===Youth and university cricket=== Singh emerged as a promising cricketer in the early 1980s, representing Delhi at Under-19 level. In 1985, he played in the [[Cooch Behar Trophy]] for Delhi Under-19 and was selected for the North Zone Under-19 squad. The following year, he was a member of the [[India national under-19 cricket team|India Under-19]] squad that toured [[Australia]] in 1986, marking his first exposure to international cricket. During his time at the [[University of Delhi]], Singh represented the Delhi University team in the [[Rohinton Baria Trophy]] in 1988 and 1989, and competed in the [[Vizzy Trophy]] Inter-University tournament for North Zone in 1989. He also represented Delhi in the [[Wills Trophy]] in 1989. ===Delhi (1986–1991)=== Singh made his first-class debut for [[Delhi cricket team|Delhi]] in the [[Ranji Trophy]] in 1986, going on to represent the state through the 1990–91 season. During this period he established himself as a reliable left-arm spinner and contributed as a lower-to-middle order batsman in Delhi's Ranji Trophy campaigns. ===Overseas professional career in England (1990–2000)=== Alongside his domestic commitments in India, Singh spent ten seasons (1990–2000) playing as an [[overseas professional]] cricketer in England. This decade-long stint gave him extensive experience in English conditions and contributed significantly to his development as a coach and administrator in later years. He qualified as a cricket coach with the [[England and Wales Cricket Board]] (ECB) in 1996 during this period. ===Assam (1996–2005)=== Singh joined the [[Assam cricket team]] for the 1996 Ranji Trophy season, having previously represented Delhi. His move to Assam proved to be the most distinguished chapter of his playing career. In the 1996 [[Ranji Trophy]] match against [[Tripura cricket team|Tripura]], he achieved the remarkable domestic feat of scoring 167 runs in an innings and taking 10 wickets in the same match — a performance that stands as a domestic all-round record.<ref name="ACA">] [added: <ref name="Bio">]{{Cite web|url= [removed: https] [added: http]:// [removed: acecricketacademy] [added: www]. [removed: in] [added: espncricinfo.com]/ [removed: the-founder] [added: ci]/ [added: content/player/34493.html]|title= [removed: About the Founder –] Sukhvinder Singh| [added: accessdate=11 April 2016 |]work= [removed: Ace Cricket Academy|accessdate=17 March 2026] [added: ESPN Cricinfo]}}</ref> [removed: He was also recognised as having the best bowling average in the country in the [[Ranji Trophy]] during the 1996–97 season. He represented East Zone in both the [[Duleep Trophy]] (2000/01) and the [[Deodhar Trophy]] (2000/01 and 2001/02), and captained the Assam Ranji Trophy side for two consecutive seasons in 2003 and 2004. He continued representing Assam in the Ranji Trophy until the 2004–05 season. ===India-B and representative cricket=== In 2001, Singh was selected to represent India-B in the [[Challenger Trophy]], playing under the captaincy of [[Sachin Tendulkar]]. He also represented [[Indian Airlines cricket team|Indian Airlines]] (now [[Air India]]) in national and international tournaments for approximately 15 years. Following his retirement from professional cricket, Singh toured Pakistan with the Indian Veterans team in 2006, and toured [[Sri Lanka]] with the Indian Veterans team in 2011. ==Coaching career== After retiring from active cricket, Singh pursued formal coaching qualifications and has since become one of Delhi's most respected cricket coaches. He holds the following certifications: * [[England and Wales Cricket Board|ECB]]-qualified cricket coach (1996) * BCCI Level 1 Coach, [[National Cricket Academy]], Bangalore (2009) * BCCI Level 2 Coach (2022) Since 2010, Singh has been the head coach and founder of '''Ace Cricket Academy''' in Rajouri Garden, New Delhi, which has grown into a prominent institution for youth cricket development in the city. ==Cricket administration== Singh has served in several key administrative roles with the [[Delhi and District Cricket Association]] (DDCA): * Selector, DDCA Under-22 (2008–09) and Under-19 (2009–10 and 2010–11) * Chairman, Junior Selection Committee, DDCA (2017–18) * Selector, Delhi Ranji Trophy and Under-23 teams (2018–19) ==Career highlights== * Member of India Under-19 squad that toured Australia (1986) * Domestic all-round record: 167 runs and 10 wickets in a single Ranji Trophy match (Assam vs. Tripura, 1996) * Best bowling average in the Ranji Trophy, 1996–97 season * Represented East Zone in the Duleep Trophy (2000/01) and the Deodhar Trophy (2000/01 and 2001/02) * Represented India-B in the Challenger Trophy under Sachin Tendulkar (2001) * Captain of the Assam Ranji Trophy team (2003 and 2004) * Ten seasons as an overseas professional cricketer in England (1990–2000) * Over 15 years representing Indian Airlines in national and international cricket] ==See also== * [[List of Delhi cricketers [removed: ]] * [[List of Assam cricketers]] * [[Ranji Trophy]] * [[Challenger Trophy (India)]] * [[Duleep Trophy]]] ==References== {{reflist}} =…

changes.text: …04/18/lauffenburger-interview-bioengineering | [removed: newspaper] [added: access-date=19 November 2020 |publisher]=The Tech |date=April 18, 2019 [added: }}</ref> He developed the basis of biological engineering curriculum at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] which heavily emphasizes quantitative and engineering based biology. He was also instrumental in the development of the Department of Biological Engineering at MIT. Lauffenburger was elected to the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 2001 “for contributions in molecular and cellular engineering and for interfacing modern biology with engineering principles.”<ref>{{cite web |title=Dr. Douglas A. Lauffenburger |url=https://www.nae.edu/29934/Dr-Douglas-A-Lauffenburger |website=National Academy of Engineering] |access-date= [removed: October 23,] [added: 11 April] 2026 [removed: }}</ref> He is also a professor in the Department of Biology (since 2002) and is affiliated with the [[Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research]] and the [[Ragon Institute]].<ref name="CV2026"/> === Biological engineering at MIT === Lauffenburger argued for a discipline in which engineers study biological systems at the level of molecular and cellular mechanisms and use that understanding to design new technologies for medicine, energy, the environment, nutrition and manufacturing, as distinct from the broader field of biomedical engineering.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> As department head he oversaw the creation of graduate programs in the late 1990s and an undergraduate major beginning in 2005; MIT describes the program as a model for similar programs elsewhere.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> He also helped launch interdisciplinary programs including the Computational and Systems Biology Initiative, the DuPont–MIT Alliance and the Cambridge–MIT Initiative.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> The National Academy of Engineering's 2021 Gordon Prize citation credited Lauffenburger and Griffith with establishing a new biology-based engineering education; Griffith led the undergraduate program and Lauffenburger the graduate level.<ref name="MITNews2021"/> === Editorial and advisory roles === Lauffenburger was editor-in-chief of ''[[Integrative Biology (journal)|Integrative Biology]]'' from 2012 to 2023 and deputy editor of ''[[PLOS Computational Biology]]'' from 2010 to 2022.<ref name="CV2026"/> He was president of the [[Biomedical Engineering Society]] in 1996–1997 and chair of the College of Fellows of the [[American Institute for Medical and Biological Engineering]] in 2001–2002.<ref name="CV2026"/> He served on the advisory council of the [[National Institute of General Medical Sciences]] from 2000 to 2004.<ref name="CV2026"/> == Research == Lauffenburger's early work, beginning in the late 1970s, used mathematical models to describe cell motility and chemotaxis, including the movement of leukocytes and bacteria.<ref name="CV2026"/> In the 1980s and 1990s he studied receptor-mediated processes such as growth factor binding and trafficking, cell adhesion and migration; this work is summarized in his book ''Receptors: Models for Binding, Trafficking, and Signaling'', co-authored with Jennifer Linderman.<ref name="MIT1995"/> Since the early 2000s his group has focused on computational and experimental analysis of cell signaling networks, using multivariate and data-driven models to relate signaling measurements to cell behaviors such as proliferation, death and migration.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> Applications have included cancer, inflammatory disease and drug resistance.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> More recent work has examined antibody responses in infectious disease and vaccination, in collaboration with immunologists including [[Galit Alter]].<ref name="CV2026"/> His group has also developed "cross-species translation" models, which use computational methods to relate findings in animal models to human data; applications include blood transcriptional correlates of BCG-mediated protection against [[tuberculosis]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bridges |first1=K. |last2=Awany |first2=D. |last3=Gela |first3=A. |last4=Lauffenburger |first4=D. kind.removed_text: (born May 6, 1953) biological engineer. He an Institute Professor and the (MIT). the founding head of MIT's Department of Biological Engineering, serving 1998 to 2019.<ref name="MITNews2026">{{cite web |last1=Trafton |first1=Anne |last2=Chu |first2=Jennifer |title=Emery Brown, Daniel Hastings, and Douglas Lauffenburger named Institute Professors |url=https://news.mit.edu/2026/emery-brown-daniel-hastings-douglas-lauffenburger-named-institute-professors-0720 |website=MIT News |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology |date=July 20, 2026 |access-date=October 23, 2026}}</ref> His research applies quantitative and computational modeling to cell signaling, and he is known for helping to establish biological engineering as a discipline distinct biomedical engineering. He is a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], and in 2021 shared the [[Bernard M. Gordon Prize]] for engineering education with [[Linda Griffith]].<ref name="MITNews2021">{{cite web |title=Linda Griffith and Douglas Lauffenburger honored for contributions to biological engineering education |url=https://news.mit.edu/2021/griffith-lauffenburger-win-gordon-prize-innovation-engineering-technology-education-0311 |website=MIT News |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology |date=March 11, 2021 |access-date=October 23, 2026}}</ref> == Early life and education == born in Des Plaines, Illinois.<ref name="CV2026">{{cite web |last=Lauffenburger |first=Douglas A. |title=Curriculum Vitae – January 2026 |url=https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.mit.edu/dist/2/2070/files/2026/01/DAL-CV-Jan-2026.pdf |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology |date=January 2026 |access-date=October 23, 2026}}</ref> He earned a B.S. in chemical engineering from Urbana-Champaign]] in 1975 and a Ph.D. in chemical engineering from Minnesota]] in 1979.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> According to MIT News, he became interested in the biological sciences while in graduate school.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> The University of Illinois later named him a distinguished alumnus (2026).<ref name="Illinois2026">{{cite web |title=Douglas Lauffenburger – 2026 Distinguished Alumni Award |url=https://chbe.illinois.edu/alumni/alumni-awards/88559 |website=Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering |publisher=University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign |access-date=October 23, 2026}}</ref> == Career == Lauffenburger began academic career in 1979 as an assistant professor of chemical engineering the [[University of Pennsylvania]], where he became associate professor in 1984 and professor and department chair in 1987.<ref name="CV2026"/> He spent 1989–1990 as Hougen Visiting Professor at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]].<ref name="CV2026"/> In 1990 he moved to the University of Illinois, where he was a professor in chemical engineering and in cell and structural biology until 1994.<ref name="CV2026"/> He joined MIT in January 1995 as a professor of chemical engineering and director of a new Center for Biomedical Engineering, with an appointment in the Harvard–MIT Division of Health Sciences and Technology.<ref name="MIT1995">{{cite web |title=MIT to establish Center for Biomedical Engineering |url=https://news.mit.edu/1995/cbe |website=MIT News |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology |date=1995 |access-date=October 23, 2026}}</ref> In 1998 he became founding co-director of MIT's Division of Bioengineering and Environmental Health, which became the Department of Biological Engineering. Whitaker Professor of Bioengineering and head of the department from 2003, and Ford Professor of Engineering from 2009.<ref name="CV2026"/> He stepped down as head in 2019 succeeded by [[Angela Belcher]].<ref name="MITTech2019">{{cite |last=Zhong |first=Vivian |newspaper=The 2019 |access-date=October 23, 2026}}</ref> is also a professor in the Department of Biology (since 2002) and is affiliated with the [[Koch for Integrative Cancer Research]] and the [[Ragon Institute]].<ref name="CV2026"/> === Biological at MIT === Lauffenburger argued for a discipline in which engineers study biological systems at the level of molecular and cellular mechanisms and use that understanding to design new technologies for medicine, energy, the environment, nutrition and manufacturing, as distinct from the broader field of biomedical engineering.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> As department head he oversaw the creation of graduate programs in the late 1990s and an undergraduate major beginning in 2005; MIT describes the program as a model for similar programs elsewhere.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> He also helped launch interdisciplinary programs including the Computational and Systems Biology Initiative, the DuPont–MIT Alliance and the Cambridge–MIT Initiative.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> The National Academy of Engineering's 2021 Gordon Prize citation credited Lauffenburger and Griffith with establishing a new biology-based engineering education; Griffith led the undergraduate program and Lauffenburger the graduate level.<ref name="MITNews2021"/> === Editorial and advisory roles === Lauffenburger was editor-in-chief of ''[[Integrative Biology (journal)|Integrative Biology]]'' from 2012 to 2023 and deputy editor of ''[[PLOS Computational Biology]]'' from 2010 to 2022.<ref name="CV2026"/> president of the [[Biomedical Engineering Society]] in 1996–1997 and chair of the College of Fellows of the [[American Institute Medical and Biological Engineering]] in 2001–2002.<ref name="CV2026"/> He served on the advisory council of the [[National Institute of General Medical Sciences]] from 2000 to 2004.<ref name="CV2026"/> == Research == Lauffenburger's early work, beginning in the late 1970s, used mathematical models to describe cell motility and chemotaxis, including the movement of leukocytes and bacteria.<ref name="CV2026"/> In the 1980s and 1990s he studied receptor-mediated processes such as growth factor binding and trafficking, cell adhesion and migration; this work is summarized in his book ''Receptors: Models for Binding, Trafficking, and Signaling'', co-authored Jennifer Linderman.<ref name="MIT1995"/> Since the early 2000s his group has focused on computational and experimental analysis of cell signaling networks, using multivariate and data-driven models to relate signaling measurements to cell behaviors such as proliferation, death and migration.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> Applications have included cancer, inflammatory disease and drug resistance.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> More recent work has examined antibody responses in infectious disease and vaccination, in collaboration with immunologists including [[Galit Alter]].<ref name="CV2026"/> His group has also developed "cross-species translation" models, which use computational methods to relate findings in animal models to human data; applications include blood transcriptional correlates of BCG-mediated protection against [[tuberculosis]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bridges |first1=K. |last2=Awany |first2=D. |last3=Gela |first3=A. |last4=Lauffenburger |first4=D. |display-authors=3 |title=Cross-species blood transcriptional correlates of BCG-mediated protection against tuberculosis include innate and adaptive immune processes |journal=JCI Insight |year=2025 |volume=10 |article-number=e194450}}</ref> and protein-network differences associated with types of [[preterm birth]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lopez Zapana |first1=P. A. |last2=DeBolt |first2=C. A. |last3=Lauffenburger |first3=D. A. |display-authors=2 |title=Protein networks are influenced by maternal BMI and differentiate preterm birth types |journal=Communications Medicine |year=2026 |volume=6 |article-number=111}}</ref> among the co-authors of a ''[[Nature Communications]]'' study of [[COVID-19]] antibody levels, from about 4,300 employees, which found that certain antibody titers tracked with functional immune stability.<ref name="Bartsch2021">{{cite journal |last1=Bartsch |first1=Yannic C. |display-authors=etal |title=Discrete |journal=Nature Communications |date=February 15, 2021 |volume=12 |issue=1 |page=1018 |doi=10.1038/s41467-021-21336-8 |pmid=33589636 |pmc=7884400 |bibcode=2021NatCo..12.1018B}}</ref><ref name="Krouse2021">{{cite news |last=Krouse |first=Sarah |title=Elon got 4,000 SpaceX workers to join a COVID-19 study. Palestinians |url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/campaigns/2022/02/israels-system-of-apartheid/ |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=Amnesty International |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-07-19 |title=World Court Finds Israel Responsible for Apartheid {{!}} Human Rights Watch |url=https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/07/19/world-court-finds-israel-responsible-apartheid |access-date=2026-11-02 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-01-07 |title=UN rights chief says Israeli policy in West Bank 'resembles apartheid system' |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly9erv6p15o |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=BBC News |language=en-GB}}</ref> ==== The Golan Heights ==== The Golan Heights was occupied by Israel during the 1967 Six-Day War, in the aftermath the area was largely depopulated,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Phillips |first=Professor Christopher |date=5 June 2014 |title=The Golan Heights: ripples of civil war in Israel’s little piece of Syria |url=https://www.chathamhouse.org/2014/06/golan-heights-ripples-civil-war-israels-little-piece-syria |url-status=live |access-date=2 November 2026 |website=Chatham House}}</ref> and the territory was subsequently governed under an Israeli military administration and settled by Israeli citizens. With the 1981 [[Golan Heights Law|Golan heights law]], Israel formally annexed the Golan heights, ended the military administration and extended Israeli civil law and administration to the territory, including the right for Israeli citizens to vote in elections there. Israeli law treats the Golan heights as a sub-district of its [[Northern District (Israel)|Northern District]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=About Northern District |url=https://www.gov.il/he/pages/police_northem_district_about |url-status=live |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=www.gov.il}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=17 July 2021 |title=District and planning institutions full map north |url=https://www.gov.il/BlobFolder/generalpage/iplan_doc2/he/District_planning_institutions_full_map_north.pdf |access-date=3 November 2026 |website=gov.il}}</ref> The [[United States]] and [[Colombia]] are the only other UN member states that recognise the Golan heights as Israeli territory.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Proclamation on Recognizing the Golan Heights as Part of the State of Israel – The White House |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/proclamation-recognizing-golan-heights-part-state-israel/ |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=10 August 2026 |title=Colombia recognizes Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights |url=https://www.gov.il/en/pages/colombia-recognizes-israeli-sovereignty-over-the-golan-heights-10-aug-2026 |url-status=live |access-date=2 Nov 2026 |website=www.gov.il}}</ref> The current population of the Golan heights is predominantly Israeli settlers, with a significant Arab [[Druze]] minority. The Druze community are not automatically eligible for Israeli citizenship, and participation in Israeli elections has historically been low but has recently increased.<ref name="Berman2022-1" /><ref>Adi Hashmonai (2026). ''From Assad to Lieberman: The israelization of the Druze in the Golan reached the polls''. [online] Haaretz. Available at: <nowiki>https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/elections/2026-10-30/ty-article-magazine/.premium/from-assad-to-lieberman-the-israelization-of-the-golan-druze-reached-the-polls/000001a1-8c94-dd03-a7bf-9ef64c2b0000</nowiki> [Accessed 2 Nov. 2026].</ref> ==== East Jerusalem ==== [[East Jerusalem]] was occupied by Israel during the 1967 Six-Day War. It was formally annexed by Israel with the [[Jerusalem Law|1980 Jerusalem law]], which integrated East Jerusalem with the administration of [[West Jerusalem]] and declared that "Jerusalem, complete and united, is the capital of Israel".<ref>BASIC-LAW: JERUSALEM THE CAPITAL OF ISRAEL, 1980, https://m.knesset.gov.il/EN/activity/documents/BasicLawsPDF/BasicLawJerusalem.pdf</ref> The United States is the only other UN member state to recognise East Jerusalem as Israeli territory.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Recognizing Jerusalem as Israel's Capital |url=https://2017-2021.state.gov/recognizing-jerusalem-as-israels-capital/ |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=United States Department of State |language=en-US}}</ref> The consensus of the rest of the international community is that states should currently abstain from establishing an official diplomatic presence in Jerusalem in the hopes that East Jerusalem can eventually serve as the capital of an independent state of Palestine.<ref>Moshe Hirsch, Deborah Housen-Couriel, Ruth Lapidoth. ''Whither Jerusalem?: Proposals and Positions Concerning the future of Jerusalem'', [[Martinus Nijhoff Publishers]], 1995. pg. 15. {{ISBN|978-90-411-0077-1}}.</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Heaney |first=Christopher |title=GA Overwhelmingly Adopts Resolution Asking Nations Not to Locate Diplomatic Missions in Jerusalem (GA/11995) |url=https://www.un.org/unispal/document/ga-overwhelmingly-adopts-resolution-asking-nations-not-to-locate-diplomatic-missions-in-jerusalem-ga11995/ |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=Question of Palestine |language=en-US}}</ref> Of the 595,000 people in East Jerusalem, 39% are Israeli settlers with full citizenship and 61% are Arab Palestinians.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Quick Facts: East Jerusalem {{!}} ALL RESOURCES {{!}} Resources {{!}} The Institute for Middle East Understanding (IMEU) |url=https://imeu.org/resources/resources/quick-facts-east-jerusalem/107 |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=imeu.org |language=en}}</ref> Only 5% of the Arab population of East Jerusalem are Israeli citizens with the rest only holding permanent residency status,<ref>Hasson, N. (2022). Just 5 percent of E. Jerusalem palestinians have received Israeli citizenship since 1967. ''Haaretz''. [online] 29 May. Available at: <nowiki>https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2022-05-29/ty-article/why-so-few-palestinians-from-jerusalem-have-israeli-citizenship/00000181-0c46-d090-abe1-ed7fefc20000</nowiki> [Accessed 2 Nov. 2026].</ref> and therefore the vast majority are ineligible to vote in Knesset elections, but they may vote in Municipal elections.<ref name="Israel_Votes-1">{{Cite web |title=How Israelis vote |url=https://www.israelvotes.org/how-it-works/voting |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=Israel Votes |language=en}}</ref> ==== The West Bank ==== The [[West Bank]] has been under Israeli occupation since the 1967 Six-Day War. In the West Bank, the administration is split between areas governed by the [[Palestinian Authority]], and areas governed by an Israeli military administration. As per the [[Oslo Accords]], the administration of the territory was divided up into Areas A, B and C.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ali |first=Mohammed Haddad,Marium |title=Ten maps to understand the occupied West Bank |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/9/16/ten-maps-to-understand-the-occupied-west-bank |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=Al Jazeera |language=en}}</ref> In [[Area A]] the civil administration and security is governed by the Palestinian Authority, and it comprises 18% of the area and 55% of the population of the West Bank. In [[Area B]] the civil administration is governed by the Palestinian Authority, and the security is governed by the Israeli Defence Forces. Area B comprises 22% of the West Bank area. In [[Area C]] both the civil and security administration is governed by Israel. The population of Area C is predominantly Israeli settlers who are Israeli citizens and therefore able to vote in Israeli elections, and it makes up 60% of the area.<ref>Dayan, L. (2026). ''Explaining the West Bank map: What are areas A, B and C?'' [online] Haaretz. Available at: <nowiki>https://www.haaretz.com/haaretz-explains/2026-08-10/ty-article-magazine/.premium/explaining-the-west-bank-map-what-are-areas-a-b-and-c/0000019f-e55e-da6c-a9df-efdec6930000</nowiki> [Accessed 2 Nov. 2026].</ref> Israel refers to the whole territory as the [[Judea and Samaria Area]],<ref>{{Cite web |date=12 February 2025 |title=Approved in preliminary reading: The term “West Bank" will be replaced by “Judea and Samaria" in all legislation pertaining to the Judea and Samaria territories |url=https://main.knesset.gov.il/en/news/pressreleases/pages/press12225q.aspx |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=main.knesset.gov.il}}</ref> but has not formally annexed the territory and fully extended Israeli civil administration to it. However, Israeli settlers are able to vote from within the territory, and their settlements are recorded no different to any other Israeli electoral locality.<ref name="Israel_Votes-1" /> ==== Gaza ==== [[Gaza Strip|Gaza]] was occupied and subsequently settled by Israel during the 1967 Six-Day War, but Israeli control of the territory was volatile and marred by conflict during the [[First Intifada|First]] and [[Second Intifada|Second Intifadas]]. Israel fully [[Israeli disengagement from the Gaza Strip|disengaged from its military occupation of the Gaza strip]] in 2005 and dismantled the Israeli settlements within the territory. In the [[2006 Palestinian legislative election|2006 Palestinian Legislative Elections]] [[Hamas]] won a plurality of the seats and took control of Gaza. In the aftermath of the [[October 7 attacks|2023 October 7th Hamas attacks]], Israel invaded the territory again during the [[Gaza war]], and it has since been under a total Israeli military occupation.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-11-02 |title=Israeli-Palestinian Conflict |url=https://www.cfr.org/global-conflict-tracker/conflict/israeli-palestinian-conflict |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=Global Conflict Tracker |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-09-28 |title=Humanitarian Situation Report {{!}} 25 September 2026 |url=https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-report-25-september-2026 |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs - Occupied Palestinian Territory |language=en}}</ref> Israel has threatened to forcefully displace the Palestinian population and to [[Proposed Israeli resettlement of the Gaza Strip|settle and annex the territory]] [[Proposed Israeli resettlement of the Gaza Strip|of Gaza]],<ref>{{Cite news |last=Tharoor |first=Ishaan |date=2024-01-05 |title=Analysis {{!}} Israeli calls for Gaza’s ethnic cleansing are only getting louder |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2024/01/05/wv-israel-hamas/ |access-date=2026-11-02 |work=The Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Graham-Harrison |first=Emma |date=2026-07-18 |title=Israeli ministers announce plans for new illegal settlements in Gaza and West Bank |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jul/18/israel-plan-new-illegal-settlements-gaza-west-bank-occupied-palestine |access-date=2026-11-03 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> but currently the population of Gaza is wholly ineligible to vote in Israeli elections. ==== Newly Israeli occupied territories since 2024 and 2026 ==== In the aftermath of the collapse of the [[Ba'athist Syria|Ba'athist regime of Syria]] in December 2024, Israeli forces occupied parts of the [[UNDOF Zone|United Nations Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF) Zone]], a buffer zone of Syrian territory East of the Golan Heights.<ref name="Carnegie_Endowment_for_International_Peace2025-1" /> In 2026 as part of the Israel-Hezbollah war, Israeli forces [[Israeli occupation of Southern Lebanon (2026)|occupied large areas of southern Lebanon]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bachega |first=Hugo |date=2026-09-02 |title=BBC travels inside occupied Lebanon as officials say Israel is expanding positions |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cge41d19gq9o |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=BBC News |language=en-GB}}</ref> Both of these regions are currently under a military administration and have not been subject to Israeli settlement, and therefore the populations are wholly ineligible to vote in Israeli elections.

[[Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute]] (MS, MS)
[[University of Florida]] (PhD) | discipline = [[Engineering education]] | known_for = MIDFIELD database, CATME Team Tools }} '''Matthew W. Ohland''' is the Dale & Suzi Gallagher Professor of Engineering Education and Associate Head of the [[School of Engineering Education]] at [[Purdue University]] in West Lafayette, Indiana. He is known for his research on team assessment, engineering student persistence and demographics, and for founding the MIDFIELD longitudinal database. ==Education== Ohland received a [[Bachelor of Arts|BA]] in Religion and a [[Bachelor of Science|BS]] in Engineering from [[Swarthmore College]] in 1989, master's degrees in Mechanical Engineering (1991) and Materials Engineering (1992) from [[Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute]], and a PhD in Civil Engineering from the [[University of Florida]] in 1996. ==Career== After completing his doctorate, Ohland served as Assistant Director of the Southeastern University Coalition for Engineering Education, headquartered at the University of Florida (1996–2000), concurrently holding an [[National Science Foundation|NSF]] Postdoctoral Fellowship in STEM Education (1998–2000). He joined [[Clemson University]] in 2000 as an Assistant Professor of General Engineering, receiving tenure and promotion to Associate Professor in 2005. In 2006 he moved to Purdue University's School of Engineering Education, where he was promoted to full Professor in 2012. He has served as Associate Head of the School since 2018 and was named the Dale & Suzi Gallagher Professor in 2020. He also held a Professorial Research Fellowship at Central Queensland University in Australia (2014–2015). ==Research== ===MIDFIELD=== In 2004, Ohland founded MIDFIELD (Multiple-Institution Database for Investigating Engineering Longitudinal Development), a widely cited database containing student records and demographics for more than one million undergraduate engineering students across multiple U.S. institutions. MIDFIELD has been used to study student persistence, graduation rates, and demographic patterns across engineering disciplines. ===CATME Team Tools=== Ohland is a co-developer of CATME (Comprehensive Assessment of Team Member Effectiveness), a web-based system for forming student teams and conducting peer evaluations using behaviorally anchored rating scales. The underlying instrument was developed with colleagues in management, psychology, and engineering and described in a 2012 paper in ''[[Academy of Management Learning & Education]]''. CATME has been used by more than two million students worldwide. CATME Team Tools received Purdue University's Class of 1922 Helping Students Learn Award in 2016. ===Teamwork and diversity in engineering=== Ohland's research also addresses gender, race, and socioeconomic factors in engineering education. Notable work includes large multi-institution studies of persistence and graduation rates by race and gender, studies of peer evaluation behavior in mixed-gender teams, and research on microaggressions in student team settings. He received the Betty Vetter Award for Research from the Women in Engineering Proactive Network in 2013 for notable achievement in research related to women in engineering. ==Leadership and service== Ohland was elected President of [[Tau Beta Pi]] Engineering Honor Society, serving from 2002 to 2006. He subsequently served as Director for District 8 (2007–2010) and as an Engineering Futures Facilitator (1996–2019), delivering more than 114 seminars to approximately 2,377 students at U.S. engineering colleges. Within the [[American Society for Engineering Education]] (ASEE), he chaired the Educational Research and Methods division (2009–2011) and has served as ASEE's representative to the [[ABET]] Engineering Accreditation Commission (2023–). In [[IEEE]], he chaired the Curriculum and Pedagogy Committee of the Educational Activities Board (2013–2015) and served on the Education Society Board of Governors (2007–2013, elected position). He is co-director of the National Effective Teaching Institute (2015–). ==Teaching== In 2015, Ohland received Purdue University's Charles B. Murphy Outstanding Undergraduate Teaching Award, described as Purdue's highest honor for exceptional undergraduate teaching by a faculty member. He was inducted into Purdue's Teaching Academy in 2012 and into the Center for Instructional Excellence [[Book of Great Teachers]] in December 2018. He received Purdue's Outstanding Faculty Mentor Award in 2022. ==Selected publications== Ohland has authored or co-authored more than 80 refereed journal articles. Representative works include: * Ohland, M.W., et al. (2008). Persistence, engagement, and migration in engineering. ''Journal of Engineering Education'', 97(3), 259–278. * Ohland, M.W., et al. (2011). Race, gender, and measures of success in engineering education. ''Journal of Engineering Education'', 100(2), 225–252. (William Elgin Wickenden Award, best paper 2011) * Ohland, M.W., et al. (2012). The Comprehensive Assessment of Team Member Effectiveness. ''Academy of Management: Learning & Education'', 11(4), 609–630. * Lord, S.M., Ohland, M.W., et al. (2022). MIDFIELD: A resource for longitudinal student record research. ''IEEE Transactions on Education'', 65(3). * Dickerson, D.A., Masta, S., Ohland, M.W., & Pawley, A.L. (2024). Is Carla grumpy? Racialized and gendered microaggression in engineering student teams. ''Journal of Engineering Education'', 113(3), 603–634. {{Infobox laboratory
| name = Accelerator Test Facility
| established = mid-1980s; operating since 1992<ref name="H2">{{cite conference |last1=Pogorelsky |first1=I. |display-authors=etal |year=2016 |title=Fulfilling the Mission of Brookhaven ATF as DOE's Flagship User Facility in Accelerator Stewardship |conference=Proc. NAPAC2016, THB2IO03 |url=https://proceedings.jacow.org/napac2016/papers/thb2io03.pdf |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref><ref name="L1">{{cite web |title=Accelerator Test Facility (ATF) |publisher=DOE Office of Science, High Energy Physics |url=https://science.osti.gov/hep/Facilities/User-Facilities/ATF |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>
| type = DOE Office of Science user facility<ref name="L3">{{cite web |last1=Shea |first1=S. B. |date=7 November 2018 |title=Meet the Director: Mark Palmer |publisher=DOE Office of Science |url=https://www.energy.gov/node/4201774 |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>
| research_field = Accelerator physics, laser physics<ref name="L1" />
| location = [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]], [[Upton, New York]], U.S.<ref name="L1" />
| operating_agency = Brookhaven National Laboratory, for the DOE Office of Science<ref name="L1" />
| director = Igor Pogorelsky<ref name="O5">{{cite web |title=Igor Pogorelsky |type=staff page |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/staff/igorp |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>
| website = {{URL|https://www.bnl.gov/atf/}}
}}
The '''Accelerator Test Facility''' ('''ATF''') is a user facility for research in accelerator and laser science at [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]] (BNL) in [[Upton, New York]]. It provides users with a high-brightness electron beam of up to 80 MeV, [[Infrared|near-infrared]] lasers, and a picosecond [[Carbon-dioxide laser|carbon dioxide laser]] at 9.2 ¬µm with a peak power of up to 5 TW, all synchronized with each other<ref name="L1" /><ref name="F6">{{cite web |title=Accelerator Test Facility |website=Accelerator Test Facility |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/atf/ |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>. [[Claudio Pellegrini]] and Robert Palmer founded the ATF in the mid-1980s<ref name="H1">{{cite web |last1=Zierler |first1=D. |date=2 April 2020 |title=Interview of Claudio Pellegrini |publisher=AIP Niels Bohr Library & Archives |url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/44380 |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref><ref name="H2" />. It began operating in 1992<ref name="L1" /> and was designated a [[Office of Science|DOE Office of Science]] [[National User Facility|User Facility]] in 2015<ref name="L3" />. About half of its users come from universities<ref name="L3" />. They have tested new methods of particle acceleration, [[Free-electron laser|free-electron lasers]] and electron-beam techniques<ref name="O11">{{cite web |title=Completed Experiments |website=Accelerator Test Facility |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/atf/experiments/completed.php |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>. The ATF is funded by the High Energy Physics program of the [[United States Department of Energy|U.S. Department of Energy]] (DOE)<ref name="L2">{{cite web |author1=U.S. Department of Energy |year=2025 |title=FY 2026 Congressional Budget Justification: High Energy Physics |url=https://sc-drcds.osti.gov/-/media/budget/pdf/sc-budget-request-to-congress/2026/FY-2026-High-Energy-Physics-Budget-Request.pdf |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>.

=== History ===

==== Founding and construction ====

After Claudio Pellegrini returned from a year at [[CERN]] in 1985‚Äì86, he and Robert Palmer started the ATF at BNL and became its first co-directors<ref name="H1" /><ref name="H2" />. It was planned as a facility for research on high-brightness electron beams, free-electron lasers and laser acceleration of particles<ref name="H1" /><ref name="H3">{{cite conference |last1=Batchelor |first1=K. |display-authors=etal |year=1989 |title=Operational Status of the Brookhaven National Laboratory Accelerator Test Facility |conference=Proc. 1989 Particle Accelerator Conference, p. 273 |url=https://epaper.kek.jp/p89/PDF/PAC1989_0273.PDF |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>. BNL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program funded it in 1989‚Äì1990<ref name="H14">{{cite conference |year=2002 |title=The BNL Accelerator Test Facility: 10 years of service |format=slides |conference=ATF Users' Meeting 2002 |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/atf/meetings/usermtg/2002/ilan.pdf |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>. By 1989 the [[Electron gun|electron gun]] had been built and tested. The [[Linear particle accelerator|linac]] was driven by a [[Klystron|klystron]] system from the [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory|Stanford Linear Accelerator Center]] (SLAC), and its accelerating sections came from the [[Institute of High Energy Physics]] in Beijing<ref name="H3" />. Pellegrini traveled to Beijing to finalize this agreement. The size of the building limited the linac energy to about 70 MeV. Pellegrini moved to the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] (UCLA) in 1989<ref name="H1" />, and [[Ilan Ben-Zvi]] became head of the ATF later that year<ref name="H15">{{cite news |date=2 April 1999 |work=Brookhaven Bulletin |volume=53 |issue=11 |title=Brookhaven Bulletin, vol. 53, no. 11 |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/bnlweb/pubaf/bulletin/files/1999/19990402.pdf |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>.

==== Start of operations ====

The experimental program began in early 1991 at a beam energy of about 4 MeV<ref name="H5">{{cite conference |last1=Ben-Zvi |first1=I. |year=1991 |title=The BNL accelerator test facility and experimental program |conference=Proc. 1991 IEEE Particle Accelerator Conference, pp. 550‚Äì554 |doi=10.1109/PAC.1991.164362}}</ref>. The DOE dates the start of operations to 1992<ref name="L1" />. From the start the ATF was operated as a user facility<ref name="H5" />, although the formal DOE designation came only in 2015<ref name="L3" />. Groups from national laboratories, universities and industry proposed experiments, and a steering committee of BNL's Center for Accelerator Physics decided which to approve<ref name="H5" />. In 2001 its users came from 11 universities and 2 small businesses, from the U.S., Russia, Japan and Taiwan<ref name="H13">{{cite journal |last=Ben-Zvi |first=I. |date=July 2001 |title=Accelerator Test Facility Hosts User-Oriented Research |type=letter |journal=Physics Today |volume=54 |issue=7 |page=14 |doi=10.1063/1.1397383}}</ref>. Funding came from the DOE offices of High Energy Physics and Basic Energy Sciences<ref name="H16">{{cite web |date=March 2014 |title=Accelerator Test Facility |type=fact sheet |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/newsroom/factsheets/files/pdf/accelerator-test-facility.pdf |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>.

==== DOE Office of Science User Facility ====

On April 1, 2013, the ATF moved within BNL from the Physics Department to the Collider-Accelerator Department<ref name="Ed2">{{cite magazine |editor=C. Swinson |date=July 2013 |title=ATF Newsletter, Summer 2013 |magazine=ATF Newsletter |pages=1‚Äì2 |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/atf/docs/atfnewsletter_july2013.pdf |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>. In May 2013 the DOE asked BNL for a proposal to upgrade the ATF, to be reviewed alongside proposals from SLAC (FACET-II) and [[Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory|Fermilab]] (ASTA). The proposal was presented at a DOE review in October 2013<ref name="Ed1">{{cite magazine |title=Special Issue: 17th ATF Users' Meeting |magazine=ATF Newsletter |date=19 December 2014 |page=3 |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/atf/docs/atfnewsletter_19dec2014_usersmeetingreport.pdf |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref><ref name="S1">{{cite magazine |title=Winter 2013/14 |magazine=ATF Newsletter |date=January 2014 |page=2 |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/atf/docs/atfnewsletter_jan2014.pdf |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref><ref name="H21">{{cite report |date=c. 2013 |title=Upgrade and Operate the Accelerator Test Facility |type=proposal to DOE |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/atf/docs/atfupgrade.pdf |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>. This review led to the ATF's designation as a formal user facility.

In 2014 the DOE set up the Accelerator Stewardship program, which supports accelerator research for uses beyond particle physics<ref name="H7">{{cite web |title=Accelerator Stewardship |publisher=DOE Office of Science, Accelerator R&D and Production |url=https://science.osti.gov/ardap/ARDAP-Programs/Research-and-Development/Accelerator-Stewardship |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>. In February 2014 it funded the first stage of the upgrade, "ATF-II"<ref name="Ed1" />. By late 2014 the DOE had identified the ATF as the program's flagship facility<ref name="S3">{{cite magazine |title=Special Issue: ATF Upgrade Workshop |magazine=ATF Newsletter |date=25 November 2014 |pages=8‚Äì9, 12 |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/atf/docs/atfnewsletter_25nov2014_worshopreport.pdf |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref><ref name="Ed1" />, and in 2015 it designated the ATF an Office of Science User Facility<ref name="H6">{{cite web |last1=Eure |first1=J. |date=19 May 2015 |title=Brookhaven Lab's Accelerator Test Facility Named a DOE Office of Science User Facility |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory Newsroom |url=https://www.bnl.gov/newsroom/news.php?a=25637 |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref><ref name="L3" />.

==== Recent developments ====

In 2020 the Accelerator Stewardship program moved to the DOE's new Office of Accelerator R&D and Production<ref name="H7" />. From fiscal year 2026 that office's work was merged back into High Energy Physics, which now supports the ATF together with SLAC's FACET-II<ref name="H10">{{cite web |author1=U.S. Department of Energy |year=2025 |title=FY 2026 Office of Science Budget in Brief |url=https://sc-drcds.osti.gov/-/media/budget/pdf/sc-budget-request-to-congress/2026/FY-2026-Office-of-Science-Budget-in-Brief-BIB.pdf |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref><ref name="L2" />. In 2025 the ATF was one of the facilities in the first year of BeamNetUS, a DOE network of accelerator test facilities at six national laboratories<ref name="H11">{{cite conference |last1=Li |first1=W. |display-authors=etal |year=2025 |title=BeamNetUS at Brookhaven National Laboratory |conference=Proc. NAPAC2025, THP015 |url=https://indico.jacow.org/event/97/contributions/10833/ |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref><ref name="H22">{{cite web |title=beamNetUS |website=beamnetus.org |url=https://www.beamnetus.org/ |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref><ref name="O4">{{cite web |title=Accelerator Facilities Division |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/afd/ |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>.

=== Organization and access ===

Researchers get beam time by submitting proposals to the ATF Program Advisory Committee, which reviews them for scientific merit<ref name="O1">{{cite web |title=Program Advisory Committee |website=Accelerator Test Facility |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/atf/pac.php |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>. The ATF director appoints the committee's chair and members for five-year terms<ref name="O1" />. The committee meets each year at the ATF Users' Meeting, where running experiments also report their progress<ref name="Ed1" />. The 27th Users' Meeting took place in 2025<ref name="O3">{{cite web |title=27th ATF Users' Meeting, 29 April ‚Äì 1 May 2025 |website=BNL Indico |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://indico.bnl.gov/event/27435/ |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref><ref name="F6" />. Academic and government users pay nothing for beam time, while proprietary industrial work pays full cost<ref name="O2">{{cite web |title=Accelerator Test Facility |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/accelerators/atf.php |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>.

In fiscal year 2024 the ATF provided 2,531 hours of beam time to 83 users<ref name="L2" />. In 2017 a workshop of outside experts assessed the facility's scientific needs<ref name="H8">{{cite report |editor=B. Carlsten |date=November 2017 |title=ATF Scientific Needs Workshop Report |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/atf/docs/atf_snw_report_final.pdf |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>. Science planning workshops followed in 2019 and 2024<ref name="O12">{{cite web |title=ATF Science Planning Workshop 2019, 15‚Äì17 October 2019 |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/atfspw/events/ |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref><ref name="O13">{{cite web |title=ATF Science Planning Workshop 2024 |date=June 2024 |website=BNL Indico |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://indico.bnl.gov/event/23307/ |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>. An Accelerator Readiness Review, scheduled for fiscal year 2023<ref name="L4">{{cite web |author1=U.S. Department of Energy |date=March 2024 |title=FY 2025 Congressional Budget Justification: Accelerator R&D and Production |url=https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2024-03/FY2025-PresidentsRequest-ARDAP-1.pdf |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>, was completed successfully in August 2026. At BNL, the ATF is part of the Accelerator Facilities Division<ref name="O4" />. It is a member of the Society for Science at User Research Facilities<ref name="F6" />.

=== Education ===

The number of PhD theses based on research at the ATF grew from 15 in 2001<ref name="H13" /> to 36 in 2014<ref name="Ed1" /> and 39 in 2016<ref name="H2" />, and exceeded 50 by 2026. Two [[University of Southern California]] (USC) theses, for example, covered the current filamentation instability and the seeded self-modulation instability<ref name="Ed2" /><ref name="E28">Allen, B. Yakimenko, V. Babzien, M. Fedurin, M. Kusche, K. {{cite journal |last1=Muggli |first1=P. |year=2012 |title=Experimental Study of Current Filamentation Instability |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=109 |page=185007 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.109.185007}}</ref><ref name="E11">{{cite journal |last1=Fang |first1=Y. |display-authors=etal |year=2014 |title=Seeding of Self-Modulation Instability of a Long Electron Bunch in a Plasma |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=112 |page=045001 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.112.045001}}</ref>. From 2015, the Center for Accelerator Science and Education, a joint venture of [[Stony Brook University]] and BNL, taught a graduate laboratory course at the ATF. Eight students took it in its first semester, each doing eight experiments on the facility<ref name="Ed3">{{cite magazine |title=Spring 2015 |magazine=ATF Newsletter |date=2015 |page=6 |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/atf/docs/atfnewsletter_spring2015.pdf |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>. The ATF also runs summer training programs; in 2025, 27 students spent ten weeks training on its accelerator and lasers.

=== Small business users ===

Small companies use the ATF to test hardware and run experiments, some of them funded by DOE [[Small Business Innovation Research]] (SBIR) awards<ref name="S1" /><ref name="S2">{{cite magazine |title=Spring 2014 |magazine=ATF Newsletter |date=April 2014 |page=5 |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/atf/docs/atfnewsletter_april2014.pdf |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>. Around 2013 they used 14% of the beam time<ref name="H21" />. RadiaBeam Technologies tested beam diagnostics and a dechirper at the ATF<ref name="S1" />, took part in dielectric wakefield experiments<ref name="E8">{{cite journal |last1=Andonian |first1=G. |display-authors=etal |year=2017 |title=Generation of Ramped Current Profiles in Relativistic Electron Beams Using Wakefields in Dielectric Structures |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=118 |page=054802 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.118.054802}}</ref>, and used an SBIR award for an inverse Compton X-ray source with laser recirculation<ref name="S2" />. Euclid Techlabs led the dielectric dechirper experiment<ref name="E6">{{cite journal |last1=Antipov |first1=S. |display-authors=etal |year=2014 |title=Experimental Demonstration of Energy-Chirp Compensation by a Tunable Dielectric-Based Structure |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=112 |page=114801 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.112.114801}}</ref>. STI Optronics led several laser acceleration experiments, including inverse [[Cherenkov radiation|Cherenkov]] acceleration<ref name="E47">{{cite journal |last1=Kimura |first1=W. D. |display-authors=etal |year=1995 |title=Laser Acceleration of Relativistic Electrons Using the Inverse Cherenkov Effect |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=74 |page=546 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.74.546}}</ref> and STELLA<ref name="E15">{{cite journal |last1=Kimura |first1=W. D. |display-authors=etal |year=2001 |title=First Staging of Two Laser Accelerators |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=86 |page=4041 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.86.4041}}</ref>. At the 2014 ATF upgrade workshop, small-business users asked for faster approval of short experiments, such as those funded by SBIR<ref name="S3" />. The ATF responded with off-cycle, fast-track approval of feasibility studies.

=== Facility ===

==== Electron gun and linac ====

The ATF's founders chose a [[Photoinjector|photocathode RF gun]], a type then being developed at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory|Los Alamos]]<ref name="H1" />. In this type of gun, a short laser pulse releases electrons from a cathode inside an RF cavity<ref name="H3" />. The BNL version is a 1.5-cell, 2.856 GHz ([[S band|S-band]]) cavity that gives a beam of about 5 MeV<ref name="H3" />. It was developed by Batchelor et al.<ref name="F1">{{cite conference |last1=Batchelor |first1=K. |display-authors=etal |year=1988 |title=Development of a high brightness electron gun for the Accelerator Test Facility at Brookhaven National Laboratory |conference=Proc. EPAC 1988, Rome, pp. 954‚Äì958 |url=https://epaper.kek.jp/e88/PDF/EPAC1988_0954.PDF |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>. It was the first S-band photoinjector, in 1989<ref name="F2">{{cite arXiv |last=Travier |first=C. |year=1994 |title=High-Brightness Photocathode Electron Sources |eprint=acc-phys/9411004}}</ref>. By 1994 the BNL design had been reproduced or adapted about ten times, at laboratories such as CERN, UCLA and [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]]<ref name="F2" /><ref name="F3">{{cite conference |last1=Braun |first1=H. H. |display-authors=etal |year=1996 |title=Results from the CLIC Test Facility |conference=Proc. EPAC 1996, TUY01T |url=https://epaper.kek.jp/e96/PAPERS/ORALS/TUY01T.PDF |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>. BNL, SLAC and UCLA then completed a 1.6-cell version and built four copies<ref name="F4">{{cite journal |last1=Dowell |first1=D. H. |display-authors=etal |year=2008 |title=The Development of the Linac Coherent Light Source RF Gun |journal=ICFA Beam Dynamics Newsletter |issue=46 |arxiv=1503.05877}}</ref>. Other laboratories adopted this design, among them [[Tsinghua University]]<ref name="F5">{{cite conference |last1=Du |first1=Y. |display-authors=etal |year=2007 |title=Status of the Photocathode RF Gun at Tsinghua University |conference=Proc. PAC07, TUPMN053 |url=https://proceedings.jacow.org/p07/PAPERS/TUPMN053.PDF |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>. The ATF also developed metal [[Photocathode|photocathodes]] of copper, magnesium and niobium<ref name="H12">{{cite magazine |last=Ben-Zvi |first=I. |date=3 October 2004 |title=A machine for learning |magazine=CERN Courier |url=https://cerncourier.com/a/a-machine-for-learning/ |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>.

As of 2025, the linac accelerates electrons to up to 80 MeV<ref name="L1" />. Its bunches are shorter than a picosecond and can be sent to either of two beamlines<ref name="F6" />.

==== Lasers ====

Users have two near-infrared lasers. One is a [[Nd:YAG laser]] at 1064 nm and 532 nm, which also illuminates the photocathode; the other is a [[Titanium-sapphire laser|Ti:sapphire laser]] giving compressed pulses of up to 100 mJ and shorter than 75 fs<ref name="F13">{{cite web |title=Laser Systems |website=Accelerator Test Facility |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/atf/capabilities/laser-systems.php |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>. Experiments can combine them with the electron beam and the CO‚ÇÇ laser<ref name="F6" />.

The long-wave infrared CO‚ÇÇ laser works at 9.2 ¬µm. Isotopically enriched amplifiers allowed it to amplify picosecond pulses without splitting them<ref name="E5">Polyanskiy, M. N. Pogorelsky, I. V. {{cite journal |last1=Yakimenko |first1=V. |year=2011 |title=Picosecond pulse amplification in isotopic CO‚ÇÇ active medium |journal=Optics Express |volume=19 |pages=7717‚Äì7725 |doi=10.1364/OE.19.007717}} {{cite journal |last1=Polyanskiy |first1=M. N. |display-authors=etal |year=2021 |title=High-peak-power long-wave infrared lasers with CO‚ÇÇ amplifiers |journal=Photonics |volume=8 |page=101 |doi=10.3390/photonics8040101}} {{cite journal |last1=Polyanskiy |first1=M. N. |display-authors=etal |year=2021 |title=Ultrashort-pulse, terawatt, long-wave infrared lasers based on high-pressure CO‚ÇÇ amplifiers |journal=EPJ Web of Conferences |volume=255 |page=11010 |doi=10.1051/epjconf/202125511010}}</ref>. In 2015 the ATF reported the first [[Chirped pulse amplification|chirped-pulse amplification]] in a CO‚ÇÇ laser<ref name="F7">{{cite magazine |title=Summer 2015 |magazine=ATF Newsletter |date=2015 |page=6 |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/atf/docs/ATFNewsletter_Summer2015.pdf |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>. In 2020 it reached 5 TW in 2 ps pulses<ref name="F8">Polyanskiy, M. N. Pogorelsky, I. V. Babzien, M. {{cite journal |last1=Palmer |first1=M. A. |year=2020 |title=Demonstration of a 2 ps, 5 TW peak power, long-wave infrared laser based on chirped-pulse amplification with mixed-isotope CO‚ÇÇ amplifiers |journal=OSA Continuum |volume=3 |page=459 |doi=10.1364/OSAC.381467}}</ref>, of which about half is delivered to users<ref name="F9">{{cite arXiv |last1=Power |first1=J. |display-authors=etal |year=2022 |title=Beam Test Facilities for R&D in Accelerator Science and Technologies (Snowmass 2021 report) |eprint=2203.11290}}</ref>. In 2024, nonlinear compression shortened the pulses to 675 fs at 1.6 TW<ref name="F10">{{cite journal |last1=Pogorelsky |first1=I. |display-authors=etal |year=2024 |title=Terawatt-class femtosecond long-wave infrared laser |journal=Frontiers in Physics |volume=12 |page=1390225 |doi=10.3389/fphy.2024.1390225}}</ref>.

==== Beam instrumentation ====

Techniques developed at the ATF include slice-emittance measurement<ref name="E2">Qiu, X. Batchelor, K. Ben-Zvi, I. {{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=X.-J. |year=1996 |title=Demonstration of Emittance Compensation through the Measurement of the Slice Emittance of a 10-ps Electron Bunch |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=76 |page=3723 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.76.3723}}</ref>, and bunch-length and [[Beam emittance|emittance]] measurement from [[Shot noise|shot-noise]] fluctuations in incoherent radiation<ref name="F11">{{cite journal |last1=Catravas |first1=P. |display-authors=etal |year=1999 |title=Measurement of Electron-Beam Bunch Length and Emittance Using Shot-Noise-Driven Fluctuations in Incoherent Radiation |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=82 |page=5261 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.82.5261}}</ref>. Another was a high-precision [[Tomography|tomography]] method for mapping the beam's phase space<ref name="F12">Yakimenko, V. Babzien, M. {{cite journal |last1=Ben-Zvi |first1=I. |display-authors=etal |year=2003 |title=Electron beam phase-space measurement using a high-precision tomography technique |journal=Phys. Rev. ST Accel. Beams |volume=6 |page=122801 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevSTAB.6.122801}}</ref>.

=== Research ===

ATF users have used the facility to test new methods of particle acceleration, beam manipulation and radiation generation.

==== Electron beam physics ====

In 1996 the BNL photocathode gun produced 370 fs bunches of 2.5√ó10‚Å∏ electrons with a normalized emittance of 0.5œÄ mm mrad<ref name="E1">Wang, X. J. Qiu, X. {{cite journal |last1=Ben-Zvi |first1=I. |year=1996 |title=Experimental observation of high-brightness microbunching in a photocathode rf electron gun |journal=Phys. Rev. E |volume=54 |page=R3121 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.54.R3121}}</ref>. The same year, Qiu and co-workers measured the emittance of a picosecond slice of a 10 ps bunch, and used it to show emittance compensation directly<ref name="E2" />. Muggli and co-workers placed a wire mask in a dispersive section to turn the beam into trains of sub-picosecond micro-bunches with adjustable spacing; the method was later used to drive multi-bunch [[Plasma acceleration|plasma wakefield]] experiments<ref name="E3">Muggli, P. Yakimenko, V. Babzien, M. Kallos, E. {{cite journal |last1=Kusche |first1=K. P. |year=2008 |title=Generation of Trains of Electron Microbunches with Adjustable Subpicosecond Spacing |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=101 |page=054801 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.101.054801}}</ref>. In 2012 [[Avraham Gover|Gover]] and co-workers reported suppression of the beam's current noise below the shot-noise level at optical frequencies<ref name="E4">Gover, A. Nause, A. Dyunin, E. {{cite journal |last1=Fedurin |first1=M. |year=2012 |title=Beating the shot-noise limit |journal=Nature Physics |volume=8 |pages=877‚Äì880 |doi=10.1038/nphys2443}}</ref>. In 2012 Yakimenko and co-workers showed that metal shielding plates suppress the energy spread caused by coherent synchrotron radiation<ref name="E35">{{cite journal |last1=Yakimenko |first1=V. |display-authors=etal |year=2012 |title=Experimental Observation of Suppression of Coherent-Synchrotron-Radiation‚ÄìInduced Beam-Energy Spread with Shielding Plates |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=109 |page=164802 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.109.164802}}</ref>.

==== Laser development ====

In 2011 the ATF laser group showed that an isotopically enriched CO‚ÇÇ gain medium removes the splitting of 5 ps pulses in the regenerative amplifier. This made terawatt picosecond CO‚ÇÇ pulses possible<ref name="E5" />. The ATF then applied chirped-pulse amplification to the CO‚ÇÇ laser, reporting it as the first use of the technique in a CO‚ÇÇ laser<ref name="F7" />. This shortened the pulses to 2 ps and raised the peak power to 5 TW<ref name="F8" />. In 2024 nonlinear compression gave 675 fs pulses at 1.6 TW<ref name="F10" />.

==== Dielectric wakefield structures ====

In 2012 a team led by Euclid Techlabs used the beam's own wakefield in a dielectric structure to modulate its energy at terahertz frequencies<ref name="E34">{{cite journal |last1=Antipov |first1=S. |display-authors=etal |year=2012 |title=Experimental Observation of Energy Modulation in Electron Beams Passing through Terahertz Dielectric Wakefield Structures |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=108 |page=144801 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.108.144801}}</ref>. In 2014 the same team tested a tunable "dechirper" of two dielectric slabs on the 60 MeV beam. Adjusting the gap removed the correlated energy spread of the bunch<ref name="E6" />. A UCLA-led team used a planar structure with Bragg-reflector walls to generate single-mode coherent Cherenkov radiation at 210 GHz<ref name="E7">{{cite journal |last1=Andonian |first1=G. |display-authors=etal |year=2014 |title=Planar-Dielectric-Wakefield Accelerator Structure Using Bragg-Reflector Boundaries |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=113 |page=264801 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.113.264801}}</ref>. A UCLA and RadiaBeam team used self-wakefields in a dielectric structure, followed by a [[Magnetic chicane|chicane]], to produce a nearly linear ramped current profile<ref name="E8" />.

==== Plasma wakefield acceleration ====

In 2003 a BNL-led team accelerated and focused parts of the beam in an overdense capillary plasma, confirming the predicted 90¬∞ phase offset between the longitudinal and transverse plasma wakefields<ref name="E40">{{cite journal |last1=Yakimenko |first1=V. |display-authors=etal |year=2003 |title=Cohesive Acceleration and Focusing of Relativistic Electrons in Overdense Plasma |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=91 |page=014802 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.91.014802}}</ref>. In 2008 a USC-led team sent two sub-picosecond bunches through a capillary plasma; the trailing bunch was accelerated at 150 MeV/m in the wake of the leading one<ref name="E41">{{cite journal |last1=Kallos |first1=E. |display-authors=etal |year=2008 |title=High-Gradient Plasma-Wakefield Acceleration with Two Subpicosecond Electron Bunches |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=100 |page=074802 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.100.074802}}</ref>. In 2014 a bunch with a sharp rising edge was used to seed the self-modulation instability, a process relevant to proton-driven plasma acceleration<ref name="E11" />. A UCLA team reached plasma blowout in the quasi-nonlinear regime with a beam of about 100 A focused to about 5 ¬µm<ref name="E12">{{cite magazine |author=S. Barber |title=Quasi nonlinear plasma wakefield acceleration |magazine=ATF Newsletter (Winter 2013/14) |date=January 2014 |page=3 |publisher=Brookhaven National Laboratory |url=https://www.bnl.gov/atf/docs/atfnewsletter_jan2014.pdf |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>.

==== Laser acceleration ====

Several experiments used the ATF CO‚ÇÇ laser to accelerate the electron beam directly:

* '''Inverse Cherenkov acceleration (1995).''' A radially polarized laser pulse, focused into a hydrogen-filled cell, accelerated 40 MeV electrons by up to 3.7 MeV over 12 cm<ref name="E47" />.
* '''IFEL energy gain (1996).''' An inverse free-electron laser (IFEL) driven by a 1‚Äì2 GW CO‚ÇÇ laser pulse raised the energy of a 40 MeV beam by 2.5% over 0.47 m<ref name="E30">van Steenbergen, A. Gallardo, J. Sandweiss, J. {{cite journal |last1=Fang |first1=J.-M. |year=1996 |title=Observation of Energy Gain at the BNL Inverse Free-Electron-Laser Accelerator |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=77 |page=2690 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.77.2690}}</ref>.
* '''IFEL micro-bunching (1997).''' Coherent [[Transition radiation|transition radiation]] showed that an IFEL bunched the beam at the laser wavelength<ref name="E14">{{cite conference |last1=Liu |first1=Y. |display-authors=etal |year=1997 |title=Experimental Observation of IFEL Micro-Bunching Using Coherent Transition Radiation |conference=Proc. 1997 Particle Accelerator Conference, Vancouver, pp. 621‚Äì623 |url=https://proceedings.jacow.org/pac97/papers/pdf/3PC003.PDF |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>.
* '''Staged laser acceleration (2001).''' In the STELLA experiment, one laser drove two IFELs 2.3 m apart: the first bunched the beam and the second accelerated it<ref name="E15" />. In the follow-on STELLA-II experiment, up to 80% of the electrons were trapped and accelerated, with an energy spread as low as 0.36%<ref name="E16">{{cite journal |last1=Kimura |first1=W. D. |display-authors=etal |year=2002 |title=STELLA-II: Staged monoenergetic laser acceleration ‚Äî experiment update |journal=AIP Conf. Proc. |volume=647 |page=269 |doi=10.1063/1.1524881}}</ref><ref name="E33">{{cite journal |last1=Kimura |first1=W. D. |display-authors=etal |year=2004 |title=Demonstration of High-Trapping-Efficiency and Narrow-Energy-Spread Laser-Driven Acceleration |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=92 |page=054801 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.92.054801}}</ref><ref name="H18">{{cite magazine |date=1 March 2004 |title=...and STELLA lights way to a better electron accelerator |magazine=CERN Courier |url=https://cerncourier.com/a/and-stella-lights-way-to-a-better-electron-accelerator/ |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>.
* '''Helical IFEL.''' The UCLA RUBICON experiment used a tapered helical [[Undulator|undulator]] to reach an accelerating gradient of about 100 MV/m and an energy gain of about 50 MeV<ref name="E36">{{cite journal |last1=Duris |first1=J. |display-authors=etal |year=2014 |title=High-quality electron beams from a helical inverse free-electron laser accelerator |journal=Nature Communications |volume=5 |page=4928 |doi=10.1038/ncomms5928}}</ref>.
* '''PASER (2006).''' A [[Technion ‚Äì Israel Institute of Technology|Technion]] team accelerated a micro-bunched beam directly by [[Stimulated emission|stimulated emission]] in an excited CO‚ÇÇ gas mixture<ref name="E18">Banna, S. Berezovsky, V. {{cite journal |last1=Sch√§chter |first1=L. |year=2006 |title=Experimental Observation of Direct Particle Acceleration by Stimulated Emission of Radiation |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=97 |page=134801 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.97.134801}}</ref>.

==== Free-electron lasers ====

In 1998 ATF researchers observed [[Self-amplified spontaneous emission|self-amplified spontaneous emission]] (SASE) in a free-electron laser (FEL) with a [[Wiggler (synchrotron)|microwiggler]], at 1064 nm and 633 nm<ref name="E39">{{cite journal |last1=Babzien |first1=M. |display-authors=etal |year=1998 |title=Observation of self-amplified spontaneous emission in the near-infrared and visible wavelengths |journal=Phys. Rev. E |volume=57 |page=6093 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.57.6093}}</ref>. The later VISA FEL, a collaboration of UCLA, BNL, SLAC and [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory|LLNL]], reached SASE saturation at 840 nm<ref name="E19">{{cite book |last1=Murokh |first1=A. |display-authors=etal |year=2003 |chapter=Results of the VISA SASE FEL experiment at 840 nm |title=Free Electron Lasers 2002 |publisher=Elsevier |pages=417‚Äì421 |doi=10.1016/B978-0-444-51417-2.50098-5}}</ref><ref name="H20">{{cite web |last1=Cornacchia |first1=M. |last2=Nuhn |first2=H.-D. |last3=Pellegrini |first3=C. |year=2002 |title=VISA: A Milestone on the Path towards X-Ray Free Electron Lasers |website=SSRL Science Highlights |publisher=SLAC |url=https://www-ssrl.slac.stanford.edu/research/highlights_archive/visa.html |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>. At saturation, the second and third harmonics each carried about 1% of the energy of the fundamental<ref name="E32">{{cite journal |last1=Tremaine |first1=A. |display-authors=etal |year=2002 |title=Experimental Characterization of Nonlinear Harmonic Radiation from a Visible Self-Amplified Spontaneous Emission Free-Electron Laser at Saturation |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=88 |page=204801 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.88.204801}}</ref>. A BNL‚Äì[[Argonne National Laboratory|Argonne]] team seeded an FEL with the 10.6 ¬µm CO‚ÇÇ laser and obtained coherent output at the 5.3 ¬µm second harmonic, a scheme called high-gain harmonic generation (HGHG). The result was reported in ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' in 2000<ref name="E20">{{cite journal |last1=Yu |first1=L. H. |display-authors=etal |year=2000 |title=First lasing of a high-gain harmonic generation free-electron laser experiment |journal=Nucl. Instrum. Methods Phys. Res. A |volume=445 |pages=301‚Äì306 |doi=10.1016/S0168-9002(00)00131-5}}</ref><ref name="E31">{{cite journal |last1=Yu |first1=L. H. |display-authors=etal |year=2000 |title=High-Gain Harmonic-Generation Free-Electron Laser |journal=Science |volume=289 |page=932 |doi=10.1126/science.289.5481.932}}</ref><ref name="H19">{{cite magazine |last=Coffey-Rosich |first=V. |date=1 December 2000 |title=Harmonic-generation FEL may lead to x-rays |magazine=Laser Focus World |url=https://www.laserfocusworld.com/detectors-imaging/article/16555524/harmonicgeneration-fel-may-lead-to-xrays |access-date=2026-10-17}}</ref>.

==== Inverse Compton scattering ====

In 2000 a BNL‚ÄìJapan collaboration collided the CO‚ÇÇ laser head-on with the 60 MeV beam and produced [[X-ray|X-rays]] peaked at 1.8 √Ö, with about 7.6√ó10‚Å∂ photons per 3.5 ps pulse<ref name="E42">{{cite journal |last1=Pogorelsky |first1=I. V. |display-authors=etal |year=2000 |title=Demonstration of 8√ó10¬π‚Å∏ photons/second peaked at 1.8 √Ö in a relativistic Thomson scattering experiment |journal=Phys. Rev. ST Accel. Beams |volume=3 |page=090702 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevSTAB.3.090702}}</ref>. In 2006 a Japan‚ÄìUS collaboration observed the second harmonic of [[Thomson scattering]] of the CO‚ÇÇ laser from the electron beam<ref name="E43">{{cite journal |last1=Babzien |first1=M. |display-authors=etal |year=2006 |title=Observation of the Second Harmonic in Thomson Scattering from Relativistic Electrons |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=96 |page=054802 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.96.054802}}</ref>. A UCLA-led team later observed the laser-induced redshift and the third harmonic of [[Compton scattering#Inverse Compton scattering|inverse Compton scattering]] (ICS)<ref name="E23">{{cite conference |last1=Sakai |first1=Y. |display-authors=etal |year=2014 |title=3rd order harmonic in inverse Compton scattering |conference=CLEO: 2014 |id=paper JTh3L.3 |doi=10.1364/CLEO_AT.2014.JTh3L.3}}</ref><ref name="E24">{{cite journal |last1=Sakai |first1=Y. |display-authors=etal |year=2015 |title=Observation of redshifting and harmonic radiation in inverse Compton scattering |journal=Phys. Rev. ST Accel. Beams |volume=18 |page=060702 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevSTAB.18.060702}}</ref>, and in 2017 recorded the angle-resolved ICS spectrum in a single shot<ref name="E25">{{cite journal |last1=Sakai |first1=Y. |display-authors=etal |year=2017 |title=Single shot, double differential spectral measurements of inverse Compton scattering in the nonlinear regime |journal=Phys. Rev. Accel. Beams |volume=20 |page=060701 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevAccelBeams.20.060701}}</ref>. An Italian-led team used a single 1 ps ICS X-ray pulse to make an inline [[Phase-contrast X-ray imaging|phase-contrast image]] of a biological sample<ref name="E26">{{cite journal |last1=Oliva |first1=P. |display-authors=etal |year=2010 |title=Quantitative evaluation of single-shot inline phase contrast imaging using an inverse Compton x-ray source |journal=Appl. Phys. Lett. |volume=97 |page=134104 |doi=10.1063/1.3491430}} {{cite journal |last1=Endrizzi |first1=M. |display-authors=etal |year=2011 |title=Quantitative phase retrieval with picosecond x-ray pulses from the ATF Inverse Compton Scattering source |journal=Optics Express |volume=19 |pages=2748‚Äì2753 |doi=10.1364/OE.19.002748}}</ref>.

==== Laser‚Äìplasma physics ====

An [[Imperial College London|Imperial College]] team used the CO‚ÇÇ laser on a hydrogen gas jet to drive a [[Radiation pressure|radiation-pressure]] shock. The shock produced MeV proton beams with about 4% energy spread<ref name="E44">{{cite journal |last1=Palmer |first1=C. A. J. |display-authors=etal |year=2011 |title=Monoenergetic Proton Beams Accelerated by a Radiation Pressure Driven Shock |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=106 |page=014801 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.106.014801}}</ref>. A USC-led team observed the current filamentation instability of the electron beam in a plasma<ref name="E28" />. A UCLA-led team, using the electron beam as a probe, mapped the magnetic fields of the thermal [[Weibel instability]] in a laser-produced plasma<ref name="E29">{{cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=C. |display-authors=etal |year=2022 |title=Mapping the self-generated magnetic fields due to thermal Weibel instability |journal=Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. |volume=119 |issue=50 |page=e2211713119 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2211713119}}</ref>. In 2024 a team reported plasma electron acceleration driven by the ATF's long-wave infrared laser<ref name="E38">{{cite journal |last1=Zgadzaj |first1=R. |display-authors=etal |year=2024 |title=Plasma electron acceleration driven by a long-wave-infrared laser |journal=Nature Communications |volume=15 |page=4037 |doi=10.1038/s41467-024-48413-y}}</ref>.

==== Propagation of CO‚ÇÇ laser beams in air ====

In 2019 a UCLA-led team reported a self-guided terawatt CO‚ÇÇ laser pulse that formed a long [[Filament propagation|filament]] in air<ref name="E37">{{cite journal |last1=Tochitsky |first1=S. Ya. |display-authors=etal |year=2019 |title=Megafilament in air formed by self-guided terawatt long-wavelength infrared laser |journal=Nature Photonics |volume=13 |page=41 |doi=10.1038/s41566-018-0315-0}}</ref><ref name="E48">{{cite journal |last1=Tochitsky |first1=S. |display-authors=etal |year=2019 |title=Filamentation of long-wave infrared pulses in the atmosphere |journal=J. Opt. Soc. Am. B |volume=36 |pages=G40‚ÄìG51 |doi=10.1364/JOSAB.36.000G40}}</ref>.

==== Other uses of the CO‚ÇÇ laser ====

With Japanese [[EUV lithography|extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) lithography]] researchers, the CO‚ÇÇ laser was focused on a liquid-xenon microjet to generate 13.5 nm EUV light, with a conversion efficiency of 0.6%<ref name="E46">{{cite journal |last1=Ueno |first1=Y. |display-authors=etal |year=2007 |title=Efficient extreme ultraviolet plasma source generated by a CO‚ÇÇ laser and a liquid xenon microjet target |journal=Appl. Phys. Lett. |volume=90 |issue=19 |doi=10.1063/1.2738190}}</ref>. Protons from the ATF's laser-driven ion source were used to irradiate [[Graphene|graphene]] films; gas released from the substrate collected under the graphene and formed bubbles<ref name="E45">{{cite journal |last1=Stolyarova |first1=E. |display-authors=etal |year=2009 |title=Observation of Graphene Bubbles and Effective Mass Transport under Graphene Films |journal=Nano Letters |volume=9 |pages=332‚Äì337 |doi=10.1021/nl803087x}}</ref>.
