[[File:Information.svg|left|25px|alt=Information icon]] Hello Arafat Haque Biswas. The nature of your edits gives the impression you have an undisclosed financial stake in promoting a topic, but you have not complied with Wikipedia's [[Wikipedia:Paid-contribution disclosure|mandatory paid editing disclosure requirements]]. Paid advocacy is a category of [[Wikipedia:Conflict of interest|conflict of interest]] (COI) editing that involves being employed (or being compensated in any way) by a person, group, company or organization to promote their interests. '''Paid advocacy on Wikipedia must be disclosed even if you have not specifically been asked to edit Wikipedia.''' Undisclosed paid advocacy is prohibited by our policies on [[Wikipedia:Neutral point of view|neutral point of view]] and what [[Wikipedia:What Wikipedia is not|Wikipedia is not]] and is an especially serious type of COI; the [[Wikimedia Foundation]] regards it as a "black hat" practice akin to [[Spamdexing|black-hat search-engine optimization]].

Paid advocates are strongly discouraged from direct article editing and should instead propose changes on the [[Help:Talk pages|talk page]] of the article in question if an article exists. If the article does not exist, paid advocates are strongly discouraged from attempting to write an article at all. At best, any proposed article creation should be submitted through the [[Wikipedia:Articles for creation|articles for creation]] process, rather than directly.

Regardless, if you are receiving or expect to receive compensation for your edits, broadly construed, you are '''<u>required</u> by the [[wmf:TOU#paid-contrib-disclosure|Wikimedia Terms of Use]] to disclose your employer, client and affiliation.''' {{If temporary account|You '''must not''' make paid edits from a temporary account. You should [[Special:CreateAccount|create a full account]] and can then post such a mandatory disclosure on that account's user page.|You can post such a mandatory disclosure to your user page at [[User:Arafat Haque Biswas]].}} The template {{tl|Paid}} can be used for this purpose – e.g. in the form: {{tlc|paid|2=user=Arafat Haque Biswas|3=employer=<var>InsertName</var>|4=client=<var>InsertName</var>}}. Unfortunately, one or more of the articles you created, such as [[:User:LocusLabs/sandbox]], may not meet Wikipedia's [[Wikipedia:Core content policies|content policies]]. If you are stuck, come to the '''[[Wikipedia:Teahouse|Teahouse]]''', where experienced Wikipedians can help you through the processes.

New to Wikipedia? Please consider taking a look at [[Help:Introduction|our introductory tutorial]] or the page on [[Wikipedia:Contributing to Wikipedia|contributing to Wikipedia]]. Below are a few other good pages about article creation.

changes.text: …- plusliga.pl - 23-04-2014 [removed: </ref> As a youth international he won gold at the [[2011 FIVB Volleyball Boys' U19 World Championship]] in Argentina.<ref>[http://www.fivb.org/EN/volleyball/competitions/Junior/Men/2011/viewpressrelease.asp ''FIVB Volleyball Men's Junior World Championship 2011''] - FIVB.org</ref> At senior level, he was part of Serbia's 14-man roster for the [[2016 FIVB Volleyball World League]] final round in Kraków, where the team won its first-ever World League title.<ref>[https://worldofvolley.com/latest_news/71440/volleyball-world-league-f6-live-blog-serbia-is-the-winner.html ''Volleyball World League F6 LIVE BLOG: Serbia is the winner''] - WorldofVolley - 17-07-2016</ref> ===End of playing career=== A few months after the 2016 World League triumph, a routine medical check with the national team revealed a cardiac arrhythmia.<ref name="sportklub">{{in lang|sr}} [https://sportklub.n1info.rs/ostali-sportovi/odbojka/brdjovic-za-sk-jos-nisam-preboleo-kraj-igracke-karijere/ ''Brđović za SK: Još nisam preboleo kraj igračke karijere''] - Sport Klub - 05-01-2022</ref> He spent roughly two to three years undergoing tests and attempting to return to competition, including surgery at the Dedinje clinic in Belgrade, but never played professionally again; his last competitive season was 2016–17 with Gazprom-Yugra, at age 24.<ref name="sportklub"/><ref name="meridian2">{{in lang|sr}} [https://meridiansport.rs/ostali-sportovi/aleksa-brdovic-intervju-odbojka/ ''Aleksa Brđović čuva sećanje na oca''] - Meridian Sport</ref> ==Coaching career== In November 2021, Brđović joined the coaching staff of his hometown club, [[OK Radnički Kragujevac|Radnički Kragujevac]], under newly appointed head coach Željko Bulatović.<ref>{{in lang|sr}} [https://www.kurir.rs/sport/ostali-sportovi/3819339/promena-na-kormilu-kragujevcana-bulatovic-novi-trener-odbojkasa-radnickog ''Promena na kormilu Kragujevčana: Bulatović novi trener odbojkaša Radničkog''] - Kurir - 29-11-2021</ref> He was promoted to head coach on 24 May 2022, at age 29.<ref>{{in lang|sr}} [https://www.infokg.rs/sport/aleksa-brdjovic-novi-trener-ok-radnicki-boricemo-se-za-sam-vrh.html ''Aleksa Brđović novi trener OK Radnički: Borićemo se za sam vrh''] - InfoKG - 24-05-2022</ref> Under Brđović, Radnički won the [[Serbian Volleyball Cup|Serbian Cup]] and the [[Volleyball League of Serbia|Serbian championship]] in 2025 — the club's first league title in 15 years, since 2009–10 — followed by the club's first-ever Serbian Super Cup later that year.<ref>{{in lang|sr}} [https://www.novosti.rs/sport/ostali-sportovi/1464122/ ''Pehar dar Kragujevcu: Aleksa Brđović ponosan što je odbojkaše Radničkog vodio do trijumfa u Kupu Srbije''] - Treći trofej u 2025. godini''] - InfoKG - 2025</ref> Radnički retained the championship in 2025–26, although the club lost that season's Serbian Cup final, played in Subotica, to Spartak Subotica.<ref>{{in lang|sr}} [https://www.okradnickikg.com/radnicki-brani-trofej-u-subotici-iskustvo-i-motiv-kao-aduti-u-finalu-kupa-srbije/ ''Radnički brani trofej u Subotici: iskustvo i motiv kao aduti u finalu Kupa Srbije''] - items.removed_text: coach and former [[Kragujevac]] 18 August 2026 volleyball coach and former player. A setter, he won gold with Serbia's [[Serbia men's national volleyball team|national team]] at the [[2016 FIVB Volleyball World League]] before a heart arrhythmia ended his playing career. He later became head coach of [[OK Radnički Kragujevac|Radnički Kragujevac]], winning four trophies with the club between 2025 and 2026, and in July 2026 was named head coach of Russian Super League club Orenburg — the first foreign head coach in the club's history. a Yugoslav international captained the team to bronze at the [[1996 Summer Olympics]]. ==Playing career== Brđović began his senior career with [[OK Ribnica|Ribnica]] in 2009, before spells with [[OK Mladi Radnik|Mladi Radnik]] (2010–2011) and [[OK Partizan|Partizan]] (2011–2013).<ref name="srwiki">{{in lang|sr}} [https://sr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Алекса_Брђовић ''Алекса Брђовић''] - sr.wikipedia.org - retrieved 22-08-2026</ref> the for Russian side Surgut]] on a It proved to be his final club.<ref name="srwiki"/> Brđović for [[Serbia men's national volleyball team|Serbian national team]] in 2012 and was called up for the League|2014 World League]] squad As a youth international he won gold at the [[2011 FIVB Volleyball Boys' U19 World Championship]] in Argentina.<ref>[http://www.fivb.org/EN/volleyball/competitions/Junior/Men/2011/viewpressrelease.asp ''FIVB Volleyball Men's Junior World Championship 2011''] - FIVB.org</ref> At senior level, he was part of Serbia's 14-man roster for the [[2016 FIVB Volleyball World League]] final round in Kraków, where the team won its first-ever World League title.<ref>[https://worldofvolley.com/latest_news/71440/volleyball-world-league-f6-live-blog-serbia-is-the-winner.html ''Volleyball World League F6 LIVE BLOG: Serbia is the winner''] - WorldofVolley - 17-07-2016</ref> ===End of playing career=== A few months after the 2016 World League triumph, a routine medical check with the national team revealed a cardiac arrhythmia.<ref name="sportklub">{{in lang|sr}} [https://sportklub.n1info.rs/ostali-sportovi/odbojka/brdjovic-za-sk-jos-nisam-preboleo-kraj-igracke-karijere/ ''Brđović za SK: Još nisam preboleo kraj igračke karijere''] - Sport Klub - 05-01-2022</ref> He spent roughly two to three years undergoing tests and attempting to return to competition, including surgery at the Dedinje clinic in Belgrade, but never played professionally again; his last competitive season was 2016–17 with Gazprom-Yugra, at age 24.<ref name="sportklub"/><ref name="meridian2">{{in lang|sr}} [https://meridiansport.rs/ostali-sportovi/aleksa-brdovic-intervju-odbojka/ ''Aleksa Brđović čuva sećanje na oca''] - Meridian Sport</ref> ==Coaching career== In November 2021, Brđović joined the coaching staff of his hometown club, [[OK Radnički Kragujevac|Radnički Kragujevac]], under newly appointed head coach Željko Bulatović.<ref>{{in lang|sr}} [https://www.kurir.rs/sport/ostali-sportovi/3819339/promena-na-kormilu-kragujevcana-bulatovic-novi-trener-odbojkasa-radnickog ''Promena na kormilu Kragujevčana: Bulatović novi trener odbojkaša Radničkog''] - Kurir - 29-11-2021</ref> He was promoted to head coach on 24 May 2022, at age 29.<ref>{{in lang|sr}} [https://www.infokg.rs/sport/aleksa-brdjovic-novi-trener-ok-radnicki-boricemo-se-za-sam-vrh.html ''Aleksa Brđović novi trener OK Radnički: Borićemo se za sam vrh''] - InfoKG - 24-05-2022</ref> Under Brđović, Radnički won the [[Serbian Volleyball Cup|Serbian Cup]] and the [[Volleyball League of Serbia|Serbian championship]] in 2025 — the club's first league title in 15 years, since 2009–10 — followed by the club's first-ever Serbian Super Cup later that year.<ref>{{in lang|sr}} [https://www.novosti.rs/sport/ostali-sportovi/1464122/ ''Pehar dar Kragujevcu: Aleksa Brđović ponosan što je odbojkaše Radničkog vodio do trijumfa u Kupu Srbije''] - Novosti - 2025</ref><ref>{{in lang|sr}} [https://www.infokg.rs/sport/odbojkasi-radnickog-prvi-put-u-istoriji-osvojili-superkup-srbije-treci-trofej-u-2025-godini.html ''Odbojkaši Radničkog prvi put u istoriji osvojili Superkup Srbije - Treći trofej u 2025. godini''] - InfoKG - 2025</ref> Radnički retained the championship in 2025–26, although the club lost that season's Serbian Cup final, played in Subotica, to Spartak Subotica.<ref>{{in lang|sr}} [https://www.okradnickikg.com/radnicki-brani-trofej-u-subotici-iskustvo-i-motiv-kao-aduti-u-finalu-kupa-srbije/ ''Radnički brani trofej u Subotici: iskustvo i motiv kao aduti u finalu Kupa Srbije''] - OK Radnički Kragujevac, official site</ref> In July 2026, Brđović was appointed head coach of Russian Super League club Orenburg, becoming the first foreign head coach in the club's history; his predecessor, Anton Volovik, remained with the club as his assistant.<ref>[https://www.championat.com/volleyball/news-6473466-32-letnij-serb-brdzhovich-naznachen-glavnym-trenerom-orenburzhya.html ''32-letniy serb Brdzhovich naznachen glavnym trenerom Orenburzhya''] - Championat.com - 25-07-2026</ref><ref>[https://56.ru/text/sport/2026/07/25/76552852/ ''Novyy glavnyy trener «Orenburzhya» Aleksa Brdzhovich priekhal v Orenburg''] - 56.ru - 25-07-2026</ref> '''2011''' [[File:Gold medal with cup.svg|16px]] [[2011 FIVB Volleyball Boys' U19 World Championship|U19 World Championship]] * ===As coach, with Radnički Kragujevac=== * '''2024/2025''' [[File:Gold medal with cup.svg|16px]] Serbian Cup * '''2024/2025''' [[File:Gold medal with cup.svg|16px]] Serbian Championship * '''2025''' [[File:Gold medal with cup.svg|16px]] Serbian Super Cup (club's first) * '''2025/2026''' [[File:Gold medal with cup.svg|16px]] Serbian Championship [[Category:Sportspeople from Kragujevac]]

items.removed_text: was born in County Durham, England in 1947. He now lives in Sydney, Australia and Australian citizen. He was Professor of Politics and International Relations at the University of New South Wales from 1996 until retirement in 2012. He has a long-time interest in the philosophy of Ludwig Wittgenstein, its implications for the practice of social science, and its relationship Karl Marx’s philosophical ideas. ==Academic and fiction work== Early in his career Kitching worked in the inter-disciplinary field of Development Studies, wrote a best-selling introductory text, ''Development and Underdevelopment in Historical Perspective'' (1989). He specialised in the study of economic and political development in Africa. His Oxford D Phil thesis was a participant observation study of peasant agriculture in a northern Tanzanian village, and in 1981 he Herskovitz Award of the US African Studies Association for his book ''Class and Economic Change in Kenya''. This was a widely praised study of the commercialisation of peasant agriculture in Kenya and its effects on the country’s African population. In the late conducted field research in Russia the de-collectivisation of agriculture following the collapse of the USSR. Following his retirement from academic life Gavin has continued to write about the importance of Wittgenstein’s ideas for social scientists and researchers. He has written history of football (soccer) in the North-East of England, his region of birth. As well as his academic books and articles, Kitching has also written some fiction (both and plays) and these listed below. However, although he is proud of his academic publications, which are are widely recognised and appreciated, he would not make similar claims for his fiction. He played [[]first-class cricket]] [removed: er] [added: for [[Assam cricket team|Assam]]] and [removed: cricket coach. A left-arm [[orthodox spin]]ner and left-handed middle-order batsman, he played first-class cricket for] [[Delhi cricket team|Delhi]] [added: between 1986] and [removed: [[Assam cricket team|Assam]] across two decades, representing India at the Under-19 level and competing in all of India's premier domestic tournaments] [added: 2005]. [removed: He is also widely recognised for his decade-long career as an [[overseas professional]] cricketer in England and his subsequent career as a [[BCCI]]-certified coach and cricket administrator. ==Early life and education== Singh was born on 23 February 1967 in [[Jalandhar]], Punjab, India. He completed his secondary education at Sardar Patel Vidyalaya, New Delhi (CBSE, 1986), and later graduated from [[SGTB Khalsa College]], [[University of Delhi]]. ==Playing career== ===Youth and university cricket=== Singh emerged as a promising cricketer in the early 1980s, representing Delhi at Under-19 level. In 1985, he played in the [[Cooch Behar Trophy]] for Delhi Under-19 and was selected for the North Zone Under-19 squad. The following year, he was a member of the [[India national under-19 cricket team|India Under-19]] squad that toured [[Australia]] in 1986, marking his first exposure to international cricket. During his time at the [[University of Delhi]], Singh represented the Delhi University team in the [[Rohinton Baria Trophy]] in 1988 and 1989, and competed in the [[Vizzy Trophy]] Inter-University tournament for North Zone in 1989. He also represented Delhi in the [[Wills Trophy]] in 1989. ===Delhi (1986–1991)=== Singh made his first-class debut for [[Delhi cricket team|Delhi]] in the [[Ranji Trophy]] in 1986, going on to represent the state through the 1990–91 season. During this period he established himself as a reliable left-arm spinner and contributed as a lower-to-middle order batsman in Delhi's Ranji Trophy campaigns. ===Overseas professional career in England (1990–2000)=== Alongside his domestic commitments in India, Singh spent ten seasons (1990–2000) playing as an [[overseas professional]] cricketer in England. This decade-long stint gave him extensive experience in English conditions and contributed significantly to his development as a coach and administrator in later years. He qualified as a cricket coach with the [[England and Wales Cricket Board]] (ECB) in 1996 during this period. ===Assam (1996–2005)=== Singh joined the [[Assam cricket team]] for the 1996 Ranji Trophy season, having previously represented Delhi. His move to Assam proved to be the most distinguished chapter of his playing career. changes.text: …04/18/lauffenburger-interview-bioengineering | [removed: newspaper] [added: access-date=19 November 2020 |publisher]=The Tech |date=April 18, 2019 [added: }}</ref> He developed the basis of biological engineering curriculum at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]] which heavily emphasizes quantitative and engineering based biology. He was also instrumental in the development of the Department of Biological Engineering at MIT. Lauffenburger was elected to the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 2001 “for contributions in molecular and cellular engineering and for interfacing modern biology with engineering principles.”<ref>{{cite web |title=Dr. Douglas A. Lauffenburger |url=https://www.nae.edu/29934/Dr-Douglas-A-Lauffenburger |website=National Academy of Engineering] |access-date= [removed: October 23,] [added: 11 April] 2026 [removed: }}</ref> He is also a professor in the Department of Biology (since 2002) and is affiliated with the [[Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research]] and the [[Ragon Institute]].<ref name="CV2026"/> === Biological engineering at MIT === Lauffenburger argued for a discipline in which engineers study biological systems at the level of molecular and cellular mechanisms and use that understanding to design new technologies for medicine, energy, the environment, nutrition and manufacturing, as distinct from the broader field of biomedical engineering.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> As department head he oversaw the creation of graduate programs in the late 1990s and an undergraduate major beginning in 2005; MIT describes the program as a model for similar programs elsewhere.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> He also helped launch interdisciplinary programs including the Computational and Systems Biology Initiative, the DuPont–MIT Alliance and the Cambridge–MIT Initiative.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> The National Academy of Engineering's 2021 Gordon Prize citation credited Lauffenburger and Griffith with establishing a new biology-based engineering education; Griffith led the undergraduate program and Lauffenburger the graduate level.<ref name="MITNews2021"/> === Editorial and advisory roles === Lauffenburger was editor-in-chief of ''[[Integrative Biology (journal)|Integrative Biology]]'' from 2012 to 2023 and deputy editor of ''[[PLOS Computational Biology]]'' from 2010 to 2022.<ref name="CV2026"/> He was president of the [[Biomedical Engineering Society]] in 1996–1997 and chair of the College of Fellows of the [[American Institute for Medical and Biological Engineering]] in 2001–2002.<ref name="CV2026"/> He served on the advisory council of the [[National Institute of General Medical Sciences]] from 2000 to 2004.<ref name="CV2026"/> == Research == Lauffenburger's early work, beginning in the late 1970s, used mathematical models to describe cell motility and chemotaxis, including the movement of leukocytes and bacteria.<ref name="CV2026"/> In the 1980s and 1990s he studied receptor-mediated processes such as growth factor binding and trafficking, cell adhesion and migration; this work is summarized in his book ''Receptors: Models for Binding, Trafficking, and Signaling'', co-authored with Jennifer Linderman.<ref name="MIT1995"/> Since the early 2000s his group has focused on computational and experimental analysis of cell signaling networks, using multivariate and data-driven models to relate signaling measurements to cell behaviors such as proliferation, death and migration.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> Applications have included cancer, inflammatory disease and drug resistance.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> More recent work has examined antibody responses in infectious disease and vaccination, in collaboration with immunologists including [[Galit Alter]].<ref name="CV2026"/> His group has also developed "cross-species translation" models, which use computational methods to relate findings in animal models to human data; applications include blood transcriptional correlates of BCG-mediated protection against [[tuberculosis]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bridges |first1=K. |last2=Awany |first2=D. |last3=Gela |first3=A. |last4=Lauffenburger |first4=D. A. |display-authors=3 |title=Cross-species blood transcriptional correlates of BCG-mediated protection against tuberculosis include innate and adaptive immune processes |journal=JCI Insight |year=2025 |volume=10 |article-number=e194450}}</ref> and protein-network differences associated with types of [[preterm birth]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lopez Zapana |first1=P. items.removed_text: (born May 6, 1953) biological engineer. He an Institute Professor and the (MIT). the founding head of MIT's Department of Biological Engineering, serving 1998 to 2019.<ref name="MITNews2026">{{cite web |last1=Trafton |first1=Anne |last2=Chu |first2=Jennifer |title=Emery Brown, Daniel Hastings, and Douglas Lauffenburger named Institute Professors |url=https://news.mit.edu/2026/emery-brown-daniel-hastings-douglas-lauffenburger-named-institute-professors-0720 |website=MIT News |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology |date=July 20, 2026 |access-date=October 23, 2026}}</ref> His research applies quantitative and computational modeling to cell signaling, and he is known for helping to establish biological engineering as a discipline distinct biomedical engineering. He is a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], and in 2021 shared the [[Bernard M. Gordon Prize]] for engineering education with [[Linda Griffith]].<ref name="MITNews2021">{{cite web |title=Linda Griffith and Douglas Lauffenburger honored for contributions to biological engineering education |url=https://news.mit.edu/2021/griffith-lauffenburger-win-gordon-prize-innovation-engineering-technology-education-0311 |website=MIT News |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology |date=March 11, 2021 |access-date=October 23, 2026}}</ref> == Early life and education == born in Des Plaines, Illinois.<ref name="CV2026">{{cite web |last=Lauffenburger |first=Douglas A. |title=Curriculum Vitae – January 2026 |url=https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.mit.edu/dist/2/2070/files/2026/01/DAL-CV-Jan-2026.pdf |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology |date=January 2026 |access-date=October 23, 2026}}</ref> He earned a B.S. in chemical engineering from Urbana-Champaign]] in 1975 and a Ph.D. in chemical engineering from Minnesota]] in 1979.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> According to MIT News, he became interested in the biological sciences while in graduate school.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> The University of Illinois later named him a distinguished alumnus (2026).<ref name="Illinois2026">{{cite web |title=Douglas Lauffenburger – 2026 Distinguished Alumni Award |url=https://chbe.illinois.edu/alumni/alumni-awards/88559 |website=Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering |publisher=University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign |access-date=October 23, 2026}}</ref> == Career == Lauffenburger began academic career in 1979 as an assistant professor of chemical engineering the [[University of Pennsylvania]], where he became associate professor in 1984 and professor and department chair in 1987.<ref name="CV2026"/> He spent 1989–1990 as Hougen Visiting Professor at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]].<ref name="CV2026"/> In 1990 he moved to the University of Illinois, where he was a professor in chemical engineering and in cell and structural biology until 1994.<ref name="CV2026"/> He joined MIT in January 1995 as a professor of chemical engineering and director of a new Center for Biomedical Engineering, with an appointment in the Harvard–MIT Division of Health Sciences and Technology.<ref name="MIT1995">{{cite web |title=MIT to establish Center for Biomedical Engineering |url=https://news.mit.edu/1995/cbe |website=MIT News |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology |date=1995 |access-date=October 23, 2026}}</ref> In 1998 he became founding co-director of MIT's Division of Bioengineering and Environmental Health, which became the Department of Biological Engineering. Whitaker Professor of Bioengineering and head of the department from 2003, and Ford Professor of Engineering from 2009.<ref name="CV2026"/> He stepped down as head in 2019 succeeded by [[Angela Belcher]].<ref name="MITTech2019">{{cite |last=Zhong |first=Vivian |newspaper=The 2019 |access-date=October 23, 2026}}</ref> is also a professor in the Department of Biology (since 2002) and is affiliated with the [[Koch for Integrative Cancer Research]] and the [[Ragon Institute]].<ref name="CV2026"/> === Biological at MIT === Lauffenburger argued for a discipline in which engineers study biological systems at the level of molecular and cellular mechanisms and use that understanding to design new technologies for medicine, energy, the environment, nutrition and manufacturing, as distinct from the broader field of biomedical engineering.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> As department head he oversaw the creation of graduate programs in the late 1990s and an undergraduate major beginning in 2005; MIT describes the program as a model for similar programs elsewhere.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> He also helped launch interdisciplinary programs including the Computational and Systems Biology Initiative, the DuPont–MIT Alliance and the Cambridge–MIT Initiative.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> The National Academy of Engineering's 2021 Gordon Prize citation credited Lauffenburger and Griffith with establishing a new biology-based engineering education; Griffith led the undergraduate program and Lauffenburger the graduate level.<ref name="MITNews2021"/> === Editorial and advisory roles === Lauffenburger was editor-in-chief of ''[[Integrative Biology (journal)|Integrative Biology]]'' from 2012 to 2023 and deputy editor of ''[[PLOS Computational Biology]]'' from 2010 to 2022.<ref name="CV2026"/> president of the [[Biomedical Engineering Society]] in 1996–1997 and chair of the College of Fellows of the [[American Institute Medical and Biological Engineering]] in 2001–2002.<ref name="CV2026"/> He served on the advisory council of the [[National Institute of General Medical Sciences]] from 2000 to 2004.<ref name="CV2026"/> == Research == Lauffenburger's early work, beginning in the late 1970s, used mathematical models to describe cell motility and chemotaxis, including the movement of leukocytes and bacteria.<ref name="CV2026"/> In the 1980s and 1990s he studied receptor-mediated processes such as growth factor binding and trafficking, cell adhesion and migration; this work is summarized in his book ''Receptors: Models for Binding, Trafficking, and Signaling'', co-authored Jennifer Linderman.<ref name="MIT1995"/> Since the early 2000s his group has focused on computational and experimental analysis of cell signaling networks, using multivariate and data-driven models to relate signaling measurements to cell behaviors such as proliferation, death and migration.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> Applications have included cancer, inflammatory disease and drug resistance.<ref name="MITNews2026"/> More recent work has examined antibody responses in infectious disease and vaccination, in collaboration with immunologists including [[Galit Alter]].<ref name="CV2026"/> His group has also developed "cross-species translation" models, which use computational methods to relate findings in animal models to human data; applications include blood transcriptional correlates of BCG-mediated protection against [[tuberculosis]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bridges |first1=K. |last2=Awany |first2=D. |last3=Gela |first3=A. |last4=Lauffenburger |first4=D. |display-authors=3 |title=Cross-species blood transcriptional correlates of BCG-mediated protection against tuberculosis include innate and adaptive immune processes |journal=JCI Insight |year=2025 |volume=10 |article-number=e194450}}</ref> and protein-network differences associated with types of [[preterm birth]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lopez Zapana |first1=P. A. |last2=DeBolt |first2=C. A. |last3=Lauffenburger |first3=D. A. |display-authors=2 |title=Protein networks are influenced by maternal BMI and differentiate preterm birth types |journal=Communications Medicine |year=2026 |volume=6 |article-number=111}}</ref> among the co-authors of a ''[[Nature Communications]]'' study of [[COVID-19]] antibody levels, from about 4,300 employees, which found that certain antibody titers tracked with functional immune stability.<ref name="Bartsch2021">{{cite journal |last1=Bartsch |first1=Yannic C. |display-authors=etal |title=Discrete |journal=Nature Communications |date=February 15, 2021 |volume=12 |issue=1 |page=1018 |doi=10.1038/s41467-021-21336-8 |pmid=33589636 |pmc=7884400 |bibcode=2021NatCo..12.1018B}}</ref><ref name="Krouse2021">{{cite news |last=Krouse |first=Sarah |title=Elon got 4,000 SpaceX workers to join a COVID-19 study. Here's what he learned |url=https://www.foxbusiness.com/technology/elon-musk-got-4000-spacex-workers-to-join-a-covid-19-study-heres-what-he-learned |work=[[The Wall Street Journal]] |via=Fox Business |date=February 21, 2021 |access-date=February 21, 2021}}</ref> === Selected publications === * {{cite journal |last1=Palecek |first1=S. B. |title=A systems model of signaling identifies a molecular basis set for cytokine-induced apoptosis |journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |year=2005 |volume=310 |pages=1646–1653}} * {{cite journal |last1=Miller-Jensen |first1=K. |last2=Janes |first2=K. A. |last3=Brugge |first3=J. |last4=Lauffenburger |first4=D. A. |title=Common effector processing mediates cell-specific responses to stimuli |journal=Nature |year=2007 |volume=448 |pages=604–608}} * {{cite journal |last1=Zhao |first1=B. |last2=Sedlak |first2=J. P. Colburn Award, [[American Institute of Chemical Engineers]] (1988)<ref name="MIT1995"/> * Guggenheim Fellowship, [[John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation]] (1989)<ref name="CV2026"/> * C. W. McGraw Research Award, [[American Society for Engineering Education]] (1992)<ref name="MIT1995"/> * Member, [[National Academy of Engineering]] (2001), "for contributions in molecular and cellular engineering and for interfacing modern biology with engineering principles"<ref>{{cite web |title=Dr. Lauffenburger |url=https://www.nae.edu/29934/Dr-Douglas-A-Lauffenburger |publisher=National Academy of Engineering |access-date=April 11, 2026}}</ref> * Member, [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (2001)<ref name="MITNews2026"/> * Distinguished Lectureship Award, [[Biomedical Engineering Society]] (2003)<ref>{{cite web |title=Awards and honors |url=https://news.mit.edu/2003/aandh-1022 |website=MIT News |date=October 22, 2003 |access-date=October 23, 2026}}</ref> * Pierre Galletti Award, [[American Institute for Medical and Biological Engineering]] (2007), for training bioengineering faculty, establishing MIT's biological engineering program, and authoring a seminal text on receptors<ref>{{cite web |title=Lauffenburger wins 2007 Galletti award |url=https://news.mit.edu/2007/lauffenburger |website=MIT News |date=2007 |access-date=October 23, 2026}}</ref> * Fellow, [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (2019)<ref>{{cite web |title=Six MIT faculty elected 2019 AAAS Fellows |url=https://news.mit.edu/2019/faculty-elected-aaas-fellows-1126 |website=MIT News |date=November 26, 2019 |access-date=February 21, 2021}}</ref> * [[Bernard M. Syria, which were occupied after the 1967 [[Six-Day War]];<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ismail |first=Ahmad |title=Territories occupied by Israel since June 1967 - Map and 2024 respectively.<ref name="Carnegie_Endowment_for_International_Peace2025-1">{{Cite web |date=2025-12-04 |title=Israel’s Ring of Buffer Zones |url=https://carnegieendowment.org/middle-east/diwan/2025/12/israels-ring-of-buffer-zones |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=Carnegie Endowment for International Peace |language=en}}</ref> The suppression of democratic self-determination of the Arab population within the Israeli occupied territories, the discriminatory parallel legal system for Arabs and Israeli citizens, and the forced displacement and illegal settlement within these regions has been described as a system of [[Israeli apartheid|Apartheid]] governance.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-02-01 |title=Israel's apartheid against Palestinians |url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/campaigns/2022/02/israels-system-of-apartheid/ |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=Amnesty International |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-07-19 |title=World Court Finds Israel Responsible for Apartheid {{!}} Human Rights Watch |url=https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/07/19/world-court-finds-israel-responsible-apartheid |access-date=2026-11-02 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-01-07 |title=UN rights chief says Israeli policy in West Bank 'resembles apartheid system' |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly9erv6p15o |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=BBC News |language=en-GB}}</ref> ==== The Golan Heights ==== The Golan Heights was occupied by Israel during the 1967 Six-Day War, in the aftermath the area was largely depopulated,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Phillips |first=Professor Christopher |date=5 June 2014 |title=The Golan Heights: ripples of civil war in Israel’s little piece of Syria |url=https://www.chathamhouse.org/2014/06/golan-heights-ripples-civil-war-israels-little-piece-syria |url-status=live |access-date=2 November 2026 |website=Chatham House}}</ref> and the territory was subsequently governed under an Israeli military administration and settled by Israeli citizens. With the 1981 [[Golan Heights Law|Golan heights law]], Israel formally annexed the Golan heights, ended the military administration and extended Israeli civil law and administration to the territory, including the right for Israeli citizens to vote in elections there. Israeli law treats the Golan heights as a sub-district of its [[Northern District (Israel)|Northern District]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=About Northern District |url=https://www.gov.il/he/pages/police_northem_district_about |url-status=live |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=www.gov.il}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=17 July 2021 |title=District and planning institutions full map north |url=https://www.gov.il/BlobFolder/generalpage/iplan_doc2/he/District_planning_institutions_full_map_north.pdf |access-date=3 November 2026 |website=gov.il}}</ref> The [[United States]] and [[Colombia]] are the only other UN member states that recognise the Golan heights as Israeli territory.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Proclamation on Recognizing the Golan Heights as Part of the State of Israel – The White House |url=https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/presidential-actions/proclamation-recognizing-golan-heights-part-state-israel/ |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=10 August 2026 |title=Colombia recognizes Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights |url=https://www.gov.il/en/pages/colombia-recognizes-israeli-sovereignty-over-the-golan-heights-10-aug-2026 |url-status=live |access-date=2 Nov 2026 |website=www.gov.il}}</ref> The current population of the Golan heights is predominantly Israeli settlers, with a significant Arab [[Druze]] minority. The Druze community are not automatically eligible for Israeli citizenship, and participation in Israeli elections has historically been low but has recently increased.<ref name="Berman2022-1" /><ref>Adi Hashmonai (2026). ''From Assad to Lieberman: The israelization of the Druze in the Golan reached the polls''. [online] Haaretz. Available at: <nowiki>https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/elections/2026-10-30/ty-article-magazine/.premium/from-assad-to-lieberman-the-israelization-of-the-golan-druze-reached-the-polls/000001a1-8c94-dd03-a7bf-9ef64c2b0000</nowiki> [Accessed 2 Nov. 2026].</ref> ==== East Jerusalem ==== [[East Jerusalem]] was occupied by Israel during the 1967 Six-Day War. It was formally annexed by Israel with the [[Jerusalem Law|1980 Jerusalem law]], which integrated East Jerusalem with the administration of [[West Jerusalem]] and declared that "Jerusalem, complete and united, is the capital of Israel".<ref>BASIC-LAW: JERUSALEM THE CAPITAL OF ISRAEL, 1980, https://m.knesset.gov.il/EN/activity/documents/BasicLawsPDF/BasicLawJerusalem.pdf</ref> The United States is the only other UN member state to recognise East Jerusalem as Israeli territory.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Recognizing Jerusalem as Israel's Capital |url=https://2017-2021.state.gov/recognizing-jerusalem-as-israels-capital/ |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=United States Department of State |language=en-US}}</ref> The consensus of the rest of the international community is that states should currently abstain from establishing an official diplomatic presence in Jerusalem in the hopes that East Jerusalem can eventually serve as the capital of an independent state of Palestine.<ref>Moshe Hirsch, Deborah Housen-Couriel, Ruth Lapidoth. ''Whither Jerusalem?: Proposals and Positions Concerning the future of Jerusalem'', [[Martinus Nijhoff Publishers]], 1995. pg. 15. {{ISBN|978-90-411-0077-1}}.</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Heaney |first=Christopher |title=GA Overwhelmingly Adopts Resolution Asking Nations Not to Locate Diplomatic Missions in Jerusalem (GA/11995) |url=https://www.un.org/unispal/document/ga-overwhelmingly-adopts-resolution-asking-nations-not-to-locate-diplomatic-missions-in-jerusalem-ga11995/ |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=Question of Palestine |language=en-US}}</ref> Of the 595,000 people in East Jerusalem, 39% are Israeli settlers with full citizenship and 61% are Arab Palestinians.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Quick Facts: East Jerusalem {{!}} ALL RESOURCES {{!}} Resources {{!}} The Institute for Middle East Understanding (IMEU) |url=https://imeu.org/resources/resources/quick-facts-east-jerusalem/107 |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=imeu.org |language=en}}</ref> Only 5% of the Arab population of East Jerusalem are Israeli citizens with the rest only holding permanent residency status,<ref>Hasson, N. (2022). Just 5 percent of E. Jerusalem palestinians have received Israeli citizenship since 1967. ''Haaretz''. [online] 29 May. Available at: <nowiki>https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2022-05-29/ty-article/why-so-few-palestinians-from-jerusalem-have-israeli-citizenship/00000181-0c46-d090-abe1-ed7fefc20000</nowiki> [Accessed 2 Nov. 2026].</ref> and therefore the vast majority are ineligible to vote in Knesset elections, but they may vote in Municipal elections.<ref name="Israel_Votes-1">{{Cite web |title=How Israelis vote |url=https://www.israelvotes.org/how-it-works/voting |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=Israel Votes |language=en}}</ref> ==== The West Bank ==== The [[West Bank]] has been under Israeli occupation since the 1967 Six-Day War. In the West Bank, the administration is split between areas governed by the [[Palestinian Authority]], and areas governed by an Israeli military administration. As per the [[Oslo Accords]], the administration of the territory was divided up into Areas A, B and C.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ali |first=Mohammed Haddad,Marium |title=Ten maps to understand the occupied West Bank |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/9/16/ten-maps-to-understand-the-occupied-west-bank |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=Al Jazeera |language=en}}</ref> In [[Area A]] the civil administration and security is governed by the Palestinian Authority, and it comprises 18% of the area and 55% of the population of the West Bank. In [[Area B]] the civil administration is governed by the Palestinian Authority, and the security is governed by the Israeli Defence Forces. Area B comprises 22% of the West Bank area. In [[Area C]] both the civil and security administration is governed by Israel. The population of Area C is predominantly Israeli settlers who are Israeli citizens and therefore able to vote in Israeli elections, and it makes up 60% of the area.<ref>Dayan, L. (2026). ''Explaining the West Bank map: What are areas A, B and C?'' [online] Haaretz. Available at: <nowiki>https://www.haaretz.com/haaretz-explains/2026-08-10/ty-article-magazine/.premium/explaining-the-west-bank-map-what-are-areas-a-b-and-c/0000019f-e55e-da6c-a9df-efdec6930000</nowiki> [Accessed 2 Nov. 2026].</ref> Israel refers to the whole territory as the [[Judea and Samaria Area]],<ref>{{Cite web |date=12 February 2025 |title=Approved in preliminary reading: The term “West Bank" will be replaced by “Judea and Samaria" in all legislation pertaining to the Judea and Samaria territories |url=https://main.knesset.gov.il/en/news/pressreleases/pages/press12225q.aspx |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=main.knesset.gov.il}}</ref> but has not formally annexed the territory and fully extended Israeli civil administration to it. However, Israeli settlers are able to vote from within the territory, and their settlements are recorded no different to any other Israeli electoral locality.<ref name="Israel_Votes-1" /> ==== Gaza ==== [[Gaza Strip|Gaza]] was occupied and subsequently settled by Israel during the 1967 Six-Day War, but Israeli control of the territory was volatile and marred by conflict during the [[First Intifada|First]] and [[Second Intifada|Second Intifadas]]. Israel fully [[Israeli disengagement from the Gaza Strip|disengaged from its military occupation of the Gaza strip]] in 2005 and dismantled the Israeli settlements within the territory. In the [[2006 Palestinian legislative election|2006 Palestinian Legislative Elections]] [[Hamas]] won a plurality of the seats and took control of Gaza. In the aftermath of the [[October 7 attacks|2023 October 7th Hamas attacks]], Israel invaded the territory again during the [[Gaza war]], and it has since been under a total Israeli military occupation.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-11-02 |title=Israeli-Palestinian Conflict |url=https://www.cfr.org/global-conflict-tracker/conflict/israeli-palestinian-conflict |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=Global Conflict Tracker |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-09-28 |title=Humanitarian Situation Report {{!}} 25 September 2026 |url=https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-report-25-september-2026 |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs - Occupied Palestinian Territory |language=en}}</ref> Israel has threatened to forcefully displace the Palestinian population and to [[Proposed Israeli resettlement of the Gaza Strip|settle and annex the territory]] [[Proposed Israeli resettlement of the Gaza Strip|of Gaza]],<ref>{{Cite news |last=Tharoor |first=Ishaan |date=2024-01-05 |title=Analysis {{!}} Israeli calls for Gaza’s ethnic cleansing are only getting louder |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2024/01/05/wv-israel-hamas/ |access-date=2026-11-02 |work=The Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Graham-Harrison |first=Emma |date=2026-07-18 |title=Israeli ministers announce plans for new illegal settlements in Gaza and West Bank |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jul/18/israel-plan-new-illegal-settlements-gaza-west-bank-occupied-palestine |access-date=2026-11-03 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> but currently the population of Gaza is wholly ineligible to vote in Israeli elections. ==== Newly Israeli occupied territories since 2024 and 2026 ==== In the aftermath of the collapse of the [[Ba'athist Syria|Ba'athist regime of Syria]] in December 2024, Israeli forces occupied parts of the [[UNDOF Zone|United Nations Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF) Zone]], a buffer zone of Syrian territory East of the Golan Heights.<ref name="Carnegie_Endowment_for_International_Peace2025-1" /> In 2026 as part of the Israel-Hezbollah war, Israeli forces [[Israeli occupation of Southern Lebanon (2026)|occupied large areas of southern Lebanon]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bachega |first=Hugo |date=2026-09-02 |title=BBC travels inside occupied Lebanon as officials say Israel is expanding positions |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cge41d19gq9o |access-date=2026-11-02 |website=BBC News |language=en-GB}}</ref> Both of these regions are currently under a military {{hat|condense for brevity}} {{Infobox academic | name = Matthew W. Ohland | employer = Purdue University | workplaces = [[Purdue University]], [[Clemson University]] | alma_mater = [[Swarthmore College]] (BA, BS)
[[Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute]] (MS, MS)
[[University of Florida]] (PhD) | discipline = [[Engineering education]] | known_for = MIDFIELD database, CATME Team Tools }} '''Matthew W. Ohland''' is the Dale & Suzi Gallagher Professor of Engineering Education and Associate Head of the [[School of Engineering Education]] at [[Purdue University]] in West Lafayette, Indiana. He is known for his research on team assessment, engineering student persistence and demographics, and for founding the MIDFIELD longitudinal database. ==Education== Ohland received a [[Bachelor of Arts|BA]] in Religion and a [[Bachelor of Science|BS]] in Engineering from [[Swarthmore College]] in 1989, master's degrees in Mechanical Engineering (1991) and Materials Engineering (1992) from [[Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute]], and a PhD in Civil Engineering from the [[University of Florida]] in 1996. ==Career== After completing his doctorate, Ohland served as Assistant Director of the Southeastern University Coalition for Engineering Education, headquartered at the University of Florida (1996–2000), concurrently holding an [[National Science Foundation|NSF]] Postdoctoral Fellowship in STEM Education (1998–2000). He joined [[Clemson University]] in 2000 as an Assistant Professor of General Engineering, receiving tenure and promotion to Associate Professor in 2005. In 2006 he moved to Purdue University's School of Engineering Education, where he was promoted to full Professor in 2012. He has served as Associate Head of the School since 2018 and was named the Dale & Suzi Gallagher Professor in 2020. He also held a Professorial Research Fellowship at Central Queensland University in Australia (2014–2015). ==Research== ===MIDFIELD=== In 2004, Ohland founded MIDFIELD (Multiple-Institution Database for Investigating Engineering Longitudinal Development), a widely cited database containing student records and demographics for more than one million undergraduate engineering students across multiple U.S. institutions. MIDFIELD has been used to study student persistence, graduation rates, and demographic patterns across engineering disciplines. ===CATME Team Tools=== Ohland is a co-developer of CATME (Comprehensive Assessment of Team Member Effectiveness), a web-based system for forming student teams and conducting peer evaluations using behaviorally anchored rating scales. The underlying instrument was developed with colleagues in management, psychology, and engineering and described in a 2012 paper in ''[[Academy of Management Learning & Education]]''. CATME has been used by more than two million students worldwide. CATME Team Tools received Purdue University's Class of 1922 Helping Students Learn Award in 2016. ===Teamwork and diversity in engineering=== Ohland's research also addresses gender, race, and socioeconomic factors in engineering education. Notable work includes large multi-institution studies of persistence and graduation rates by race and gender, studies of peer evaluation behavior in mixed-gender teams, and research on microaggressions in student team settings. He received the Betty Vetter Award for Research from the Women in Engineering Proactive Network in 2013 for notable achievement in research related to women in engineering. ==Leadership and service== Ohland was elected President of [[Tau Beta Pi]] Engineering Honor Society, serving from 2002 to 2006. He subsequently served as Director for District 8 (2007–2010) and as an Engineering Futures Facilitator (1996–2019), delivering more than 114 seminars to approximately 2,377 students at U.S. engineering colleges. Within the [[American Society for Engineering Education]] (ASEE), he chaired the Educational Research and Methods division (2009–2011) and has served as ASEE's representative to the [[ABET]] Engineering Accreditation Commission (2023–). In [[IEEE]], he chaired the Curriculum and Pedagogy Committee of the Educational Activities Board (2013–2015) and served on the Education Society Board of Governors (2007–2013, elected position). He is co-director of the National Effective Teaching Institute (2015–). ==Teaching== In 2015, Ohland received Purdue University's Charles B. Murphy Outstanding Undergraduate Teaching Award, described as Purdue's highest honor for exceptional undergraduate teaching by a faculty member. He was inducted into Purdue's Teaching Academy in 2012 and into the Center for Instructional Excellence [[Book of Great Teachers]] in December 2018. He received Purdue's Outstanding Faculty Mentor Award in 2022. ==Selected publications== Ohland has authored or co-authored more than 80 refereed journal articles.
